name: Classic-Style Test 2
source: Original questions written for LSAT Trainer in the style and difficulty of recent LSATs. Not LSAC material. MIT licensed.

questions.stimulus: A survey of 600 adults found that those who regularly sing in a choir reported feeling lonely far less often than did those who do not sing in any group. This difference held for younger and older respondents alike. Clearly, then, joining a choir is an effective way for a person to reduce loneliness.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: overlooks the possibility that people who seldom feel lonely are more inclined than others to join a choir
draws a general conclusion about adults from a survey that included only some of the adults in the population
takes for granted that singing in a choir is the only effective way for a person to reduce loneliness
fails to establish that singing in a choir reduces loneliness more effectively than other group activities do
confuses how often people feel lonely with how intensely they feel lonely when they do
questions.explanation: The survey shows only a correlation between choir singing and low loneliness, yet the argument concludes that joining a choir reduces loneliness. It ignores reversed causation: people who are already seldom lonely may be the ones who join choirs, which is (A). (B) is tempting because the evidence is a survey, but every survey covers only some of a population, and nothing suggests this one is unrepresentative. (C) and (D) attribute claims the argument never makes: it calls choirs an effective way, not the only or the best way.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Joining a choir is an effective way for a person to reduce loneliness.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: In a survey of 600 adults, regular choir singers reported feeling lonely far less often than people who sing in no group, at every age.

breakdown.analysis: So choir singers are less lonely. Does that mean the choir made them that way? Maybe the arrow runs backwards: people who are already social and rarely lonely are the ones who sign up for a choir, while lonely people avoid group activities in the first place. It's like noticing that people at parties are less lonely and concluding parties cure loneliness. Prephrase: the argument ignores that low loneliness might lead to choir membership, not the other way around.

choices.note: CORRECT. Reversed causation. If people who are seldom lonely are more likely to join choirs, choir singers would report less loneliness even if singing did nothing at all for loneliness.

Tempting because it's a survey, but every survey covers only some of a population. Nothing suggests this sample of 600 is unrepresentative, and the age detail suggests it's fairly broad. The problem is the causal leap, not the sample.
choices.example: Example of flaw: We asked 20 people at a jazz club about their favorite music, so jazz must be the most popular genre in the country.

choices.note: The argument says a choir is "an effective way," not the only way. It never rules out other cures for loneliness.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Exercise lowers stress, so anyone who wants less stress has no choice but to exercise.

choices.note: Tempting if you read "effective" as "most effective." The argument only claims choirs are an effective way, not a better way than book clubs or bowling leagues. It never compares, so it doesn't need to.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Walking lowers blood pressure, so walking must lower it more than swimming does.

choices.note: The argument never mixes up frequency and intensity. It talks only about how often, on both sides.
choices.example: Example of flaw: She cries less often than he does, so she must feel sadness less deeply.

questions.stimulus:
Kemal: The city's new limit on short-term rentals in residential neighborhoods will lower rents. Many apartments now rented to tourists will return to the long-term market, and that added supply will push rents down.

Rosa: Some apartments will indeed return to long-term tenants, but not enough of them to bring rents down. Most of the city's short-term rentals are spare rooms in owner-occupied houses, and their owners will simply stop renting them out.
questions.stem: Kemal and Rosa disagree over whether
choices: some apartments now rented to tourists will become available to long-term tenants as a result of the limit
most of the city's short-term rentals are spare rooms in houses whose owners live in them
the limit on short-term rentals will bring about a reduction in the rents charged in the city
the city acted wisely in adopting a limit on short-term rentals in its residential neighborhoods
owners of spare rooms will stop renting them out rather than offer them to long-term tenants
questions.explanation: Kemal says the limit will lower rents; Rosa says it will not return enough apartments to bring rents down, so they disagree over (C). (A) is the trap: Rosa's "will indeed" concedes Kemal's point, so they agree on it. (B) and (E) are Rosa's claims alone, since Kemal never mentions spare rooms, and neither speaker evaluates the policy, as (D) requires.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Kemal: The limit will lower rents because many tourist apartments will return to the long-term market.; Rosa: Some apartments will return, but not enough to bring rents down, because most short-term rentals are spare rooms whose owners will just stop renting.

breakdown.analysis: Find the claim one says yes to and the other says no to. Kemal: rents will go down. Rosa: no, not enough apartments come back. That's the split. Watch Rosa's "will indeed": it's a concession, so whatever follows it is something they agree on, not a disagreement. Lesson: to disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no.

choices.note: Tempting, since it's the topic of the first sentences. But Rosa concedes it ("will indeed"). They agree here.
Rosa's claim alone. Kemal says nothing about spare rooms, so he takes no position.
CORRECT. Kemal: the limit "will lower rents." Rosa: "not enough of them to bring rents down." Yes versus no on the same question.
Neither speaker says whether the city was right. They only predict the limit's effect on rents.
Rosa's prediction alone. Kemal never discusses what owners of spare rooms will do.

questions.stimulus: In the orchards of one fruit-growing valley, the population of the native orange-banded bee has fallen sharply over the past decade, the same period during which growers there widely adopted a new fungicide. Although the fungicide's manufacturer reports that it was not designed to affect insects, the fungicide is most likely responsible for the bees' decline.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: The new fungicide controls orchard fungi more effectively than did the products that growers used before it.
Orange-banded bees visit orchard blossoms less often than several other bee species in the valley do.
Over the past decade, a parasitic mite that attacks orange-banded bees has spread throughout the valley.
In valley orchards where the new fungicide has never been used, orange-banded bee numbers have held steady.
Some growers in the valley have recently begun planting wildflowers near their orchards to attract bees.
questions.explanation: The only evidence is timing: the bees declined while the fungicide spread. (D) adds a comparison group: where the fungicide was never used, the bees did not decline, which points to the fungicide rather than a valley-wide cause. (C) is on topic but names a rival cause, so it weakens; (A), (B), and (E) say nothing about what caused the decline.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The new fungicide is most likely responsible for the orange-banded bees' decline.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The bee population fell sharply over the past decade, the same period in which growers widely adopted the fungicide.

breakdown.analysis: Two things happened at once. So what? Lots of things changed in the valley over ten years. To strengthen, show the decline tracks the fungicide: places without it, bees doing fine. It's like blaming the new office coffee for your headaches; you'd be surer if coworkers who skip the coffee aren't getting headaches. Prephrase: untreated orchards kept their bees.

choices.note: How well the fungicide kills fungi says nothing about whether it hurts bees. Irrelevant.
If anything, less blossom visiting means less exposure. It doesn't link the fungicide to the decline.
Weakens. A mite spreading over the same decade is a rival cause. On topic, wrong direction.
CORRECT. A control group. Where the fungicide was never used, bee numbers held steady. So whatever is hurting the bees is tied to treated orchards, not some valley-wide cause.
A recent response to the decline. It tells us nothing about what caused it.

questions.stimulus: Real estate agent: A house priced far below similar homes nearby is seldom the bargain it appears to be. Sellers rarely set a low price without a reason, and that reason is often a defect, such as a cracked foundation or a history of flooding, that an ordinary walkthrough will not reveal. Admittedly, some sellers simply need to sell quickly. But a buyer has no way of knowing which kind of seller he or she is dealing with.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the real estate agent's argument?
choices: A house priced far below similar homes nearby often has a defect that an ordinary walkthrough will not reveal.
Buying a home listed well under the price of comparable houses in the area is probably less advantageous than it seems.
A buyer cannot tell whether a low price reflects a hidden defect or merely a seller's need to sell quickly.
Some sellers set a low price on a house only because they need to sell it quickly.
Buyers should have any unusually low-priced house professionally inspected before they make an offer on it.
questions.explanation: The agent's first sentence is the conclusion: an unusually cheap house is seldom the bargain it seems. Everything after it supports it, and (B) restates it in different words. (A) is the trap: it borrows the stimulus's own wording, but it states the supporting premise about hidden defects, and it overstates "often" into a claim about the house. (C) is the last premise, (D) is the concession, and (E) is advice the agent never gives.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: A house priced far below similar nearby homes is seldom the bargain it appears to be.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Sellers rarely set a low price without reason; that reason is often a hidden defect; some sellers just need to sell fast (concession), but buyers can't tell which kind of seller they're dealing with.

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. Why is a cheap house seldom a bargain? Because low prices usually have a reason, often a hidden defect. And the "some sellers just need to sell quickly" point? The agent concedes it, then says the buyer can't tell the difference. All of that backs the first sentence. Watch out: the right answer won't use the agent's words. Look for the idea, not the phrasing.

choices.note: Tempting, because it repeats the stimulus's language ("far below similar homes nearby," "ordinary walkthrough will not reveal"). But it's the reason the agent gives, not the claim being argued for. A premise in familiar words is the classic wrong answer here.
CORRECT. "Seldom the bargain it appears to be" becomes "probably less advantageous than it seems." Different words, same claim, and it's the claim every other sentence supports.
This is the last premise. It explains why the concession doesn't save the bargain hunter, so it supports the conclusion rather than being it.
This is the concession ("Admittedly"). The agent grants it and then sets it aside.
Good advice, but the agent never gives it. The argument stops at "not a bargain"; it doesn't tell buyers what to do.

questions.stimulus: The town of Merriton has two pharmacies, which charge nearly identical prices for prescription drugs and accept the same insurance plans. Yet Hollins Pharmacy, which is open only on weekdays, fills far more prescriptions each month than does Cardale Pharmacy, which is open seven days a week and stays open later each evening.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain why Hollins Pharmacy fills more prescriptions than Cardale Pharmacy does?
choices: Hollins Pharmacy shares a building with the clinic where most Merriton residents see their doctors.
Most prescriptions in Merriton are filled on weekday afternoons, when both pharmacies are open.
Cardale Pharmacy employs more pharmacists than Hollins does and so can fill prescriptions more quickly.
Cardale Pharmacy also sells groceries and household goods, which draws many shoppers into the store.
Some Merriton residents have their prescriptions filled by mail-order services rather than at either pharmacy.
questions.explanation: We need some advantage of Hollins that outweighs Cardale's longer hours, given equal prices and insurance. (A) supplies one: patients leaving the clinic with a prescription can fill it in the same building. (B) is tempting, but it only cancels Cardale's advantage without giving Hollins one; (C) and (D) make the gap more puzzling, and (E) affects both pharmacies equally.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Two pharmacies charge about the same and take the same insurance; Cardale is open seven days and later each evening, but weekday-only Hollins fills far more prescriptions.

breakdown.analysis: Same prices, same insurance, Cardale has more hours, yet Hollins wins big. So Hollins must have some other edge. Location is a natural one: if Hollins is where people get prescriptions in the first place, they'll fill them there. It's like a coffee cart in a hospital lobby outselling a café down the street that's open longer. Prephrase: something draws customers to Hollins.

choices.note: CORRECT. Walk out of the doctor's office with a prescription, fill it downstairs. That's an advantage big enough to beat longer hours.
Tempting. It shows Cardale's extra hours don't matter much, but both stores are open then. It removes Cardale's edge without giving Hollins one, so we still don't know why Hollins wins.
More pharmacists and faster service should help Cardale. Deepens the puzzle.
More shoppers in Cardale should mean more chances to fill prescriptions there. Deepens the puzzle.
Mail order takes business from both pharmacies. It doesn't explain the gap between them.

questions.stimulus: At Quillon Software, an employee may work from home on a given day only if that employee's team lead has approved it in advance. Team leads approve such requests only from employees who have completed the company's security training. Moreover, an employee working from home may not access the customer database that day unless he or she uses the company's encrypted connection.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: Any Quillon employee who has completed the security training may work from home whenever he or she requests it.
Every Quillon employee who uses the company's encrypted connection on a given day is working from home that day.
Any Quillon employee who works from home on a given day must have completed the company's security training.
A Quillon employee who uses the encrypted connection does not need a team lead's approval to work from home.
Quillon's team leads approve most of the requests to work from home that they receive from trained employees.
questions.explanation: Working from home requires advance approval, and approval is given only to employees who have completed the training, so anyone working from home has completed it: (C). (A) reverses the chain, treating completed training as enough to work from home rather than as a requirement. (B) likewise reverses the encrypted-connection rule, (E) adds a frequency the rules never give, and (D) contradicts the first rule.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Work from home on a day → team lead approved in advance; 2. team lead approves → employee completed security training; 3. working from home AND accessing the customer database → uses encrypted connection.

breakdown.analysis: Chain the first two: work from home → approval → training. So anyone working from home has completed training. The third rule is a side branch about the database. Every rule gives requirements; none gives guarantees. Reversing an arrow is the classic wrong answer here.

choices.note: Reverses the chain. Training is required for approval; it doesn't guarantee approval, let alone working from home whenever you like.
Reverses the third rule. The encrypted connection is required for home database access; using it doesn't mean you're home. Office workers could use it too.
CORRECT. Work from home → approved → trained. Straight down the chain.
Contradicts rule 1. Every work-from-home day needs a team lead's approval, encrypted connection or not.
The rules say nothing about how many requests get approved. Unsupported.

questions.stimulus: Meteorologist: Our station's new forecasting model correctly predicted whether it would rain the next day on 88 percent of days last spring. The model we used before it was correct on only 74 percent of days during the previous spring. Both figures were checked against the same set of rain gauges. So the new model predicts next-day rain more accurately than the old one did.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the meteorologist's argument?
choices: Last spring's weather did not make next-day rain substantially easier to forecast than the previous spring's weather did.
It rained on about the same number of days last spring as it did during the previous spring.
The new model would also be better than the old one at predicting how much rain will fall on a given day.
The new model will be correct on at least 88 percent of days during the coming spring as well.
No other forecasting model currently available to the station is any more accurate than the new model.
questions.explanation: The two models were tested in different springs, so the comparison assumes the springs were about equally hard to forecast. (A) states that: if last spring's weather was far easier to call, the 88 percent could reflect the weather rather than the model. (B) is the trap: equal numbers of rainy days are not required, since a spring can have a different number of rainy days and still be no easier to forecast. (C), (D), and (E) go beyond the conclusion, which is only about next-day rain in the past.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The new model predicts next-day rain more accurately than the old model did.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: New model: right on 88% of days last spring; old model: right on 74% of days the spring before; both checked against the same rain gauges.

breakdown.analysis: Different models, different springs. So what if the new one scored higher? Maybe last spring was just easy: a string of obvious dry weeks makes any model look good. It's like comparing two students' scores on two different tests. We need an answer that says the two springs were comparably hard to forecast. Note the meteorologist already blocked one worry (the gauges are the same), which points to the one left open.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: last spring made next-day rain much easier to forecast. Then the jump from 74 to 88 could be the weather, not the model, and the argument falls apart.
choices.negation: Last spring's weather made next-day rain substantially easier to forecast than the previous spring's weather did.

choices.note: Tempting: it sounds like the "same conditions" answer. But difficulty isn't the number of rainy days. Negate it (a different number of rainy days) and the springs could still be equally hard to call. The negation doesn't hurt.
choices.negation: It rained on a substantially different number of days last spring than during the previous spring.

choices.note: Rainfall amounts are a different task. The conclusion is only about whether it rains. Negate it and nothing changes.
choices.negation: The new model would not be better than the old one at predicting how much rain will fall.

choices.note: The conclusion is about past accuracy, not next spring. Negated, the comparison of last two springs still stands.
choices.negation: The new model will be correct on fewer than 88 percent of days next spring.

choices.note: Other models don't matter. The claim compares only the new model and the old one.
choices.negation: Some other available model is more accurate than the new model.

questions.stimulus: Archaeologist: At the hilltop site at Varo Ridge, we found grinding stones together with charred barley grains in a layer dated to about 9,000 years ago. Grinding stones were used to process grain into flour. So the people who lived at Varo Ridge must already have been farming barley by that time, well before farming is usually thought to have reached the region.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the archaeologist's argument?
choices: The charred barley grains at Varo Ridge were dated by a method that is considered highly reliable.
Later layers at Varo Ridge contain clear evidence that barley was being cultivated near the site.
Barley is easier to grind into flour than most of the other cereal grains of the region.
Farming did not reach most other parts of the region until at least a thousand years after the Varo Ridge layer formed.
At the time the layer formed, wild barley grew in abundance on the slopes surrounding Varo Ridge.
questions.explanation: The archaeologist reads grinding stones and barley as signs of farming, but both fit equally well with people gathering and grinding wild barley. (E) makes that alternative realistic: wild barley grew right around the site. (D) is the trap: it sounds relevant because it is about when farming arrived, but it only repeats the premise that Varo Ridge would be unusually early. (A) supports the dating, (B) is about later periods, and (C) says nothing about where the barley came from.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The people of Varo Ridge were already farming barley about 9,000 years ago.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A 9,000-year-old layer holds grinding stones and charred barley; grinding stones were used to make grain into flour.

breakdown.analysis: Barley plus a grinding stone means someone ground barley. Does it mean someone planted it? Not if the barley grew wild nearby and people simply gathered it. It's like finding a fishing rod and a fish in a cabin and concluding the owner ran a fish farm. We need an answer that makes wild barley a live option.

choices.note: This props up the date. It doesn't touch the leap from grinding to farming.
Later farming says nothing about farming 9,000 years ago. If anything, it nudges toward the archaeologist's story.
So barley was convenient to grind. That doesn't tell us whether it was grown or gathered.
Tempting, since it's about when farming arrived. But the archaeologist already says Varo Ridge would be ahead of the region. This just repeats that, so it can't weaken the argument.
CORRECT. If wild barley was abundant right there, people could have gathered and ground it without farming. Grinding stones and charred grains no longer point to cultivation.

questions.stimulus: Editor: A publisher should reissue an out-of-print book only if two conditions are met. First, the author, or the author's estate if the author has died, must consent to the reissue. Second, it must be possible to correct in the new edition any factual errors that have been discovered in the book since it first appeared.
questions.stem: The principle stated by the editor most helps to justify the reasoning in which one of the following arguments?
choices: Hollis Books should reissue Meera Dahl's first novel. Dahl has consented to the reissue, and no factual errors have been discovered in the novel since it first appeared.
Lattice Press should not reissue Ana Voss's field guide, because Voss has died and much of the information in the guide has since become out of date.
Fenwick House should not reissue its 1970s cookbook, since the original edition sold poorly and there is little reason to expect that a new edition would sell any better.
Arden Press should reissue Lionel Fry's chemistry textbook despite Fry's objection, because every error found in the textbook can now be corrected in a new edition.
Grayline Press should not reissue Owen Tarr's travel memoir. Tarr's estate favors a reissue, but the errors found in the memoir since it first appeared cannot be corrected.
questions.explanation: The principle states only necessary conditions for reissuing: consent and the ability to correct errors. It can therefore justify a decision not to reissue when one condition fails, as in (E), where the errors cannot be corrected. (A) is the trap: both conditions are met, but meeting necessary conditions does not show that a book should be reissued. (B) fails because Voss's estate might consent and outdated information might be correctable; (D) concludes the opposite of what the principle requires.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Reissue an out-of-print book → author (or estate) consents AND errors found since publication can be corrected. Contrapositive: no consent OR uncorrectable errors → don't reissue.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: Look for a "should not reissue" verdict where one of the two conditions clearly fails.

breakdown.analysis: "Only if" means the principle lists requirements. It can tell you not to reissue when a requirement fails. It can never tell you to reissue. So the right answer must (1) conclude "should not reissue" and (2) show consent missing or errors uncorrectable. Lesson: meeting necessary conditions doesn't make something required.

choices.note: The trap. Both conditions are met, but necessary conditions can't justify "should reissue." They only open the door.
Tempting, since it's a "should not." But no condition is shown to fail: Voss's death doesn't rule out her estate's consent, and nothing says the outdated material couldn't be corrected.
Poor sales aren't one of the principle's conditions. The principle can't justify this verdict.
Violates the consent requirement. Fry objects, so the principle says don't reissue. This concludes the opposite.
CORRECT. The estate consents, but the errors can't be corrected. The correction condition fails, so the principle says don't reissue. Both requirements of the application are met.

questions.stimulus: Columnist: Many orchestras now ask audiences not to applaud between the movements of a symphony, and defenders of this practice say that it preserves the traditional concert experience. But in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, audiences routinely applauded between movements, and composers expected them to. So the practice, far from preserving tradition, departs from it. There may be good reasons for discouraging such applause, but fidelity to tradition is not one of them.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the columnist's argument?
choices: Being faithful to tradition is not a good reason for asking concert audiences to hold their applause until a symphony ends.
Asking audiences not to applaud between the movements of a symphony departs from, rather than preserves, traditional concert practice.
Audiences in earlier centuries routinely applauded between the movements of symphonies, as the composers of those works expected.
There are good reasons for orchestras to ask audiences not to applaud between the movements of a symphony.
Orchestras should stop asking their audiences to refrain from applauding between the movements of a symphony.
questions.explanation: The history of applause shows that the no-applause practice departs from tradition, and that in turn shows the columnist's real point: tradition cannot be the reason to keep the practice, which (A) states. (B) is the trap: it is flagged with "So," but it is an intermediate conclusion that supports the last sentence. (C) is the premise, (D) overstates a concession ("may be"), and (E) goes further than the columnist, who allows that the practice might have other merits.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Fidelity to tradition is not a good reason for discouraging applause between movements.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Earlier audiences applauded between movements and composers expected it; so the practice departs from tradition.

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. The history supports "the practice departs from tradition," and that claim supports the final sentence: so tradition can't justify the practice. The "So" sits on the middle step, which is exactly what makes it a trap. The last sentence also opens with a concession ("There may be good reasons") that you shouldn't mistake for the point.

choices.note: CORRECT. This is the final sentence in new words: whatever else might justify the practice, tradition can't. Everything else in the argument builds toward it.
Tempting, because it carries the "So." But it's a middle step: the columnist uses it to show that tradition can't justify the practice. A conclusion that supports another claim isn't the main one.
This is the historical premise. It supports the claim that the practice departs from tradition.
The columnist only grants that there "may be" good reasons. That's a concession, not a claim, and certainly not the point of the argument.
Too far. The columnist attacks one defense of the practice, not the practice itself, and even allows it may have merits.

questions.stimulus: In one coastal city, the number of summer days on which the temperature exceeds 35°C has risen steadily over the past thirty years. Over the same period, however, the number of people admitted to the city's hospitals each summer for heat-related illness has fallen, even though the city's population has grown slightly.
questions.stem: Each of the following, if true, helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above EXCEPT:
choices: Over those thirty years, the share of homes in the city with air conditioning has risen from under a fifth to nearly nine-tenths.
The city's hottest days now tend to come in late summer, after most of the tourists who once crowded the city in July have left.
Most of the people admitted to the city's hospitals for heat-related illness are admitted on days when the temperature exceeds 35°C.
Improved treatments now allow most people who seek emergency care for heat illness to be sent home the same day rather than admitted.
Over the past thirty years, a growing share of the city's elderly residents have moved to cooler inland towns.
questions.explanation: More very hot days, yet fewer heat admissions. Four choices give a reason admissions could fall despite the heat: home air conditioning (A), fewer vulnerable visitors on the hottest days (B), patients treated without admission (D), and fewer vulnerable residents (E). (C) only says the admissions cluster on the hottest days, which makes the drop more puzzling, not less. (B) and (D) take a moment: tourists are not counted in the population but are admitted to hospitals, and "admitted" is narrower than "treated."

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Days over 35°C have become more common in the city, but summer hospital admissions for heat illness have fallen, even as the population grew slightly.

breakdown.analysis: EXCEPT question: four answers explain the drop and one doesn't. Good explanations either make people less vulnerable on hot days, reduce the number of vulnerable people around, or show that sick people now end up somewhere other than an admission. Watch the two subtle ones: tourists aren't residents, and an emergency-room visit isn't an admission.

choices.note: Explains it. Far more homes have air conditioning, so far fewer people overheat even on the hot days.
Explains it, though it takes a second look. Tourists end up in the hospital but aren't counted in the population. If the hot spells now arrive after they leave, fewer vulnerable people are exposed.
CORRECT. This ties admissions to the hottest days, which are increasing. That should push admissions up, so it deepens the puzzle rather than resolving it.
Explains it. If most heat-illness patients are now treated and sent home, they never count as admissions, even if just as many people get sick.
Explains it. Elderly people are especially vulnerable to heat; fewer of them in the city means fewer admissions.

questions.stimulus: Male fireflies of each species search for mates by flashing a species-specific pattern in flight; a receptive female of the same species answers from the ground with a precisely timed reply flash. Females of a few predatory species mimic other species' female replies to lure males, which they then eat. The mimics tend to make small timing errors in their replies, so prey males that approach only after seeing several replies are eaten less often than males that fly to the first reply. However, a female left waiting will often mate with a rival male who arrives sooner. Thus, ______.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: prey males that approach only after seeing several replies probably leave more offspring than males that fly to the first reply
the predatory mimics would catch fewer males if they imitated the replies of only one prey species rather than several
the timing errors the mimics make are the only cue by which prey males can tell a mimic from a female of their own species
how much a prey male gains by delaying his approach probably depends in part on how common the mimics are where he lives
most prey males that fly to the first reply they see are eventually eaten by a mimic rather than mating with a female of their own kind
questions.explanation: Waiting has a benefit (less chance of being eaten) and a cost (losing a real female to a quicker rival). How the two balance must depend on how much danger there is to avoid, so the advantage of waiting should vary with how common mimics are: (D). (A) is the trap: it takes the survival advantage in the stimulus's own words and ignores the cost the last premise adds. (C) and (E) are too strong, and (B) is about something the stimulus never discusses.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Males flash a species pattern and receptive females answer with a timed reply; 2. some predatory females mimic other species' female replies and eat the males they lure; 3. mimics make timing errors in their replies, so males that wait for several replies are eaten less often; 4. a waiting female often mates with a rival who arrives sooner.

breakdown.analysis: The last sentence is the key: "However." Waiting for several replies protects a male from mimics but costs him mates. So is waiting a good idea? It depends on how much protection is worth, and that depends on how many mimics there are. Where mimics are rare, waiting buys little safety at a real cost. We need a completion that weighs both sides. An answer that only counts the benefit is the trap.

choices.note: Tempting: it reads like the natural ending to sentence three. But sentence four says waiting costs mates. Fewer deaths could be outweighed by lost matings, so "more offspring" doesn't follow.
The stimulus never compares mimics that copy one species' replies with mimics that copy several. Unsupported.
Too strong. Timing errors are one cue; nothing says they are the only one.
CORRECT. Waiting trades mates for safety. How good that trade is depends on how much danger there is, so the gain from waiting should vary with how common mimics are.
Too strong. Males that fly to the first reply are eaten more often than waiters, not usually eaten. "Most" is nowhere supported.

questions.stimulus: A regional bookstore chain added a café to three of its forty stores, chosen at random. Over the following year, book sales at those three stores rose 12 percent, while sales at the chain's other stores rose only 2 percent on average. The chain now plans to add cafés to all of its stores, expecting the change to raise the chain's total book sales substantially.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would provide the most support for the chain's expectation?
choices: In surveys, customers at the three stores said that they enjoyed browsing books while having coffee in the cafés.
The three stores had lower book sales than the chain's average store in the year before the cafés were installed.
The cafés earned enough from selling food and drinks to pay for the cost of installing them within a year.
Several bookstore chains that compete with this one have recently added cafés to some of their stores as well.
None of the three stores is within easy driving distance of any of the chain's other stores.
questions.explanation: The comparison with the other stores already rules out a chain-wide trend, so what remains open is where the three stores' extra sales came from. If they were drawn from nearby stores of the same chain, the chain as a whole gained little, and cafés everywhere would leave no one to draw from. (E) closes that gap: none of the three stores has a sister store nearby, so the gain was new business. (A) is the trap: customers enjoying the cafés fits the rise but says nothing about whether the chain's total grew. (B) weakens (a rebound from a bad year), and (C) and (D) are about profit and competitors.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Adding cafés to all forty stores will substantially raise the chain's total book sales.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Three randomly chosen stores got cafés; their book sales rose 12 percent while the other stores averaged 2 percent.

breakdown.analysis: Random stores and a comparison group: the obvious worries are handled. So what's left? The jump from three stores to the chain's total. If the café stores just pulled book buyers from the chain's own stores nearby, the chain gained little, and an average over 37 other stores would hide a few local losses. It's like a restaurant chain bragging that its renovated branch is packed when the branch down the street is empty. We need an answer that shows the 12 percent was new business, not borrowed business.

choices.note: Tempting: happy customers sound like support. But enjoying the café isn't buying more books, and it says nothing about whether the gain was new sales or sales taken from other stores. Irrelevant corroboration.
Weakens if anything. Stores that had a bad year tend to bounce back on their own, so part of the 12 percent might have happened without the cafés.
Profit from coffee isn't book sales. Wrong measure.
What competitors do doesn't tell us whether cafés raised this chain's book sales.

CORRECT. With no sister store nearby, the extra buyers couldn't have come from the chain's other locations. So the 12 percent was a real gain for the chain, which is what the conclusion about total sales needs.

questions.stimulus: Media critic: Some newspapers now let readers vote online on which stories receive follow-up coverage. Supporters claim that this practice makes journalism more responsive to the public. In fact, it is likely to make journalism less responsive. The stories selected this way will mostly reflect the interests of a narrow and unrepresentative group, since the readers who bother to vote are largely those already devoted to a few favorite topics.
questions.stem: The claim that the stories selected by readers' votes will mostly reflect the interests of a narrow group plays which one of the following roles in the media critic's argument?
choices: It is supported by another statement in the argument and is in turn offered in support of the argument's main conclusion.
It is the main conclusion that the media critic's argument as a whole is intended to establish.
It is a premise offered in support of the main conclusion that is not itself supported by any other statement in the argument.
It is offered in support of the claim that the readers who vote are largely devoted to a few favorite topics.
It is a claim made by supporters of the practice that the media critic's argument attempts to refute.
questions.explanation: The main conclusion is that the voting practice will make journalism less responsive. The claim about the narrow group supports that, and it is itself supported by the "since" clause about who votes, so it is an intermediate step: (A). (C) is the trap: it gets the claim's relation to the main conclusion right but misses that the claim has its own support. (B) mistakes the last sentence for the conclusion, (D) reverses the support, and (E) confuses the critic's claim with the supporters'.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Letting readers vote on follow-up coverage is likely to make journalism less responsive.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Voters are largely readers devoted to a few favorite topics; so the chosen stories will reflect a narrow, unrepresentative group.

breakdown.analysis: Find the main conclusion first: "In fact, it is likely to make journalism less responsive." Then ask what the narrow-group claim does. It supports the conclusion. Does anything support it? Yes: the "since" clause right after it. A claim that has support and also gives support is a middle step. The word order hides this, because the support comes after the claim.

choices.note: CORRECT. The "since" clause backs the claim, and the claim backs the main conclusion. Supported and supporting: an intermediate conclusion.
It's the last sentence, which is why it's tempting. But it's offered as a reason for "less responsive." That's the main point.
Tempting: it gets half right. The claim does support the main conclusion, but the "since" clause supports it, so "not itself supported" is wrong.
Backwards. The voters' devotion to a few topics is the reason for the claim, not the other way around.
The supporters say the practice makes journalism more responsive. This claim is the critic's own.

questions.stimulus: Each entry in this year's Marlow County photography contest was submitted in exactly one category, landscape or portrait. Every landscape entry that won a prize was taken with a film camera, and no entry taken with a film camera was submitted by a contestant under twenty. At least one prize this year went to an entry submitted by a contestant under twenty.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following CANNOT be true?
choices: Every portrait entry that won a prize this year was submitted by a contestant under twenty.
None of this year's entries submitted by contestants under twenty was a landscape.
No portrait entry won a prize in this year's contest.
Most of this year's prize-winning entries were landscapes taken with film cameras.
Some entries taken with film cameras did not win a prize this year.
questions.explanation: Some prize went to an entry by a contestant under twenty. Such an entry was not taken with a film camera, so it cannot be a prize-winning landscape; since every entry is a landscape or a portrait, it must be a prize-winning portrait. So (C), which says no portrait won, cannot be true. (D) is the near-miss: most winners could still be film landscapes as long as at least one winner is that portrait. (A), (B), and (E) are all possible.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Every entry is landscape or portrait, not both; 2. winning landscape → film camera; 3. film camera → not under twenty; 4. at least one winning entry came from someone under twenty.

breakdown.analysis: Start with the one fact that guarantees something exists: a winning entry from someone under twenty. Run it through the rules. Under twenty → not film (contrapositive of 3). Not film → not a winning landscape (contrapositive of 2). It won, so it's not a landscape, so it's a portrait (fact 1). So at least one portrait won. The answer that CANNOT be true denies that. Everything else just has to be possible.

choices.note: Could be true. The only portrait winner might be the young contestant's entry. Nothing forces an older portrait winner.
Could be true. Young contestants might all have entered portraits. Nothing forces any young landscape entry.
CORRECT. The young contestant's winning entry can't be film, so it can't be a winning landscape; it has to be a winning portrait. "No portrait won" is impossible.
Tempting, because winning landscapes do all use film. But "most" is fine: picture two film landscapes and one young contestant's portrait taking the prizes. Possible.
Could be true. Nothing says every film entry won. Plenty of film shots could have gone home empty-handed.

questions.stimulus: Males of a certain lizard species often perform a rapid series of push-ups while perched in the open. Some researchers believe the display serves chiefly to attract females. More likely, though, it serves chiefly to warn rival males away from a territory, since males begin displaying as soon as they claim territories in early spring, weeks before any females are receptive to mating.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Females of the species, which defend small territories of their own but never court males, perform the same push-up display.
Males that hold territories perform the push-up display far more often than do males of the species that hold no territory.
Once females become receptive in late spring, males perform the push-up display even more often than they did earlier.
In several closely related lizard species, males perform similar push-up displays that are known to attract females.
Males perform the display most often on warm, sunny days, when lizards of both sexes are at their most active.
questions.explanation: The argument picks between two functions for the display: warning rivals or attracting mates. The best support is a case that separates them. (A) does: females, which defend territories but never court, give the very same display, so the display occurs where only the territorial function can apply. (B) is the trap: territory holders do display more, but territory holders are also the males that court and mate, so it fits both hypotheses equally. (C) and (D) favor the courtship view, and (E) fits both.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The push-up display serves chiefly to warn rival males away from a territory, not to attract females.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Males start displaying when they claim territories, weeks before females are receptive.

breakdown.analysis: Two hypotheses: territory or courtship. A strengthener has to favor one over the other, not just fit the territory story. So ask of each answer: would the courtship view predict this too? Prephrase: find a situation where territory is at stake but courtship isn't, and show the display still happens. It's like deciding whether a dog barks to guard the yard or to greet guests: watch whether it barks at the mail carrier when no one's home to greet.

choices.note: CORRECT. Females defend territories but never court males, and they give the same display. Courtship can't explain that; territorial defense can. The display shows up exactly where only the territorial function is in play.

Tempting: more display where there's a territory sounds like support. But males with territories are also the ones that court and mate, so the courtship view predicts the same thing. It doesn't separate the hypotheses.
Weakens, if anything. More display once females are receptive points toward courtship.
Weakens by analogy. If similar displays attract females in related species, courtship looks more likely here too.
Fits both views. Active days mean more rivals and more females alike.

questions.stimulus: Any ancient structure aligned precisely with the summer solstice sunrise was built by people who had tracked the sun's yearly movements over many years. But no people could have tracked those movements over so long a period without some means of preserving their observations. The stone ring at Hallow Fen is aligned precisely with the solstice sunrise. Therefore, the ring's builders must have had a system of writing.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?
choices: Any people who had a system of writing also had some means of preserving their observations over many years.
The builders of the Hallow Fen ring tracked the sun's yearly movements over a period of many years.
Most peoples who preserved observations of the sun over many years did so by writing those observations down.
No people lacking a system of writing would have had any means of preserving observations over many years.
Only people who tracked the sun's movements over many years built structures aligned with the solstice sunrise.
questions.explanation: The premises chain: aligned → tracked the sun for years → had a means of preserving observations. The conclusion needs that last term to lead to writing. (D) supplies it in contrapositive form: no writing → no means of preserving observations, which is the same as preserving → writing. (A) is the trap: it links the same two terms but in the reversed direction. (C) is only a "most" bridge, and (B) and (E) restate what the premises already give.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The builders of the Hallow Fen ring had a system of writing.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Aligned with solstice sunrise → tracked sun for many years; tracked for many years → had a means of preserving observations; Hallow Fen is aligned.

breakdown.analysis: Turn sentence two into an arrow: "no one could track without preserving" means tracked → preserved. So: aligned → tracked → preserved. The conclusion says writing. Writing appears nowhere in the premises, so we need preserved → writing. The right answer may be stated backwards, as a contrapositive: not writing → not preserved says exactly the same thing.

choices.note: Tempting: same two ideas, writing and preserving. But it runs writing → preserved. We need preserved → writing. Reversed bridge.
Already follows from the premises (aligned → tracked). Adding it gets you no closer to writing.
"Most" can't guarantee the builders were in the writing majority. Too weak for a conclusion that says "must."
CORRECT. Contrapositive of preserved → writing. Plug it in: aligned → tracked → preserved → writing. The conclusion follows.
Restates the first premise. It doesn't reach writing.

questions.stimulus: Ten years ago, snowboarders accounted for 45 percent of the injured people treated at the first-aid clinic of the Haldane ski resort. Last season they accounted for only 30 percent. Over the same period, the resort required all of its snowboard instructors to complete a new safety course. Clearly, snowboarding at Haldane has become less dangerous than it was ten years ago.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: takes for granted that the new safety course for snowboard instructors is responsible for the reduction in injuries
fails to consider that snowboarders may now make up a smaller share of the resort's visitors
infers that snowboarding has become less dangerous at all ski resorts from evidence about only one resort
overlooks the possibility that skiing at Haldane has also become less dangerous over the past ten years
presumes, without providing justification, that a risk that has fallen over ten years will continue to fall in the future
questions.explanation: A falling share of the clinic's patients does not show that snowboarding became safer; if snowboarders became a smaller share of visitors, their share of injuries would fall even if each snowboarder's risk stayed the same or rose. (B) names that gap. (A) is the trap: the safety course is mentioned, but the argument never claims the course caused anything. (D) points the wrong way, and (C) and (E) describe conclusions the argument does not draw.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Snowboarding at Haldane has become less dangerous than it was ten years ago.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Snowboarders were 45% of the clinic's injured patients ten years ago and 30% last season; meanwhile, snowboard instructors took a new safety course.

breakdown.analysis: Snowboarders' share of the injuries fell. So what? A share depends on who else is on the mountain. If ten years ago half the visitors were snowboarders and now only a fifth are, then snowboarders making up 30% of injuries means they're getting hurt more per person, not less. We need an answer that says the mix of visitors may have changed. This is the percent-versus-rate confusion; know it.

choices.note: Tempting, because the course is sitting right there. But the conclusion is only that snowboarding got safer, not why. The argument never blames or credits the course.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Crime fell after the new mayor took office, so the new mayor's policies must have reduced crime.

choices.note: CORRECT. Danger is about the risk per snowboarder. If snowboarders became a smaller slice of the resort's visitors, their slice of the injuries could shrink even while each snowboarder's risk held steady or rose.
The conclusion is about Haldane only. No other resort is mentioned.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Injuries fell at our resort, so skiing has become safer everywhere.

choices.note: Wrong direction. Safer skiing would push the snowboarders' share of injuries up, not down. It's the opposite case, more skier injuries, that would explain the falling share.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Burglaries in our town fell after the new alarm law, so the law worked, overlooking that burglaries fell just as much in towns without the law.

choices.note: The argument makes no prediction. It's only about the change so far.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Accidents dropped for three years, so they will keep dropping next year.

questions.stimulus: On a certain island, every ant species that cultivates fungus keeps the interior of its nests humid, and most of the island's ant species with humid nests build those nests underground. No ant species on the island that nests underground forages at night. Even so, most of the island's fungus-cultivating ant species forage at night.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: Fewer than half of the island's ant species with humid nests cultivate fungus.
At least some of the island's fungus-cultivating ant species build their nests underground.
Most of the island's ant species that forage at night cultivate fungus.
Most of the island's ant species that keep their nests humid forage at night.
The island has more ant species with humid nests than fungus-cultivating ant species.
questions.explanation: Fungus growers are all humid-nesters, and most of them forage at night, so most of them do not nest underground. If the fungus growers were all of the humid-nesters, most humid-nesters would then nest above ground, contradicting the claim that most humid-nesters nest underground. So the fungus growers are a proper subset of the humid-nesters, and the humid-nesters must outnumber them: (E). (A) is the trap: it is the same idea stated too strongly, since the fungus growers could still be a large majority of the humid-nesters. (B) and (C) are possible but not required, and (D) is ruled out.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Fungus → humid; 2. most humid → underground; 3. underground → not night; 4. most fungus species forage at night.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase, so test for a conflict. From 3, night foragers aren't underground, so by 4 most fungus species are above ground. Now suppose the fungus species were all of the humid-nesters. Then most humid-nesters would be above ground, but fact 2 says most are underground. Contradiction. So the humid group must contain some species that don't grow fungus. Quick numbers: 100 humid species, 51 underground, 49 above. Fungus species need a majority above ground, so they can't be all 100. But 90 works (46 above, 44 below), which is why "fewer than half" goes too far. The right answer is dressed up as a count comparison, which makes it look unrelated at first.

choices.note: Tempting, because it points the right way. But it's too strong. With 100 humid species (51 underground, 49 above), 90 could grow fungus: 46 above ground, 44 below. That's a majority above ground, as required, and far more than half of the humid species.
Possible, not required. Every fungus species could nest above ground; fact 4 needs only most of them to forage at night.
Uses the stimulus's words, but nothing tells us who the night foragers are. They could be mostly species that don't grow fungus.
Contradicted. Most humid-nesters are underground, and underground species never forage at night, so most humid-nesters don't forage at night.

CORRECT. Every fungus species is a humid-nester, and they can't be all of the humid-nesters (that would clash with fact 2). So there's at least one humid-nester that doesn't grow fungus, which means humid-nesters outnumber fungus growers. The comparison hides a plain "some humid-nesters don't grow fungus."

questions.stimulus: The rail line will be extended to Orland only if the regional council approves new funding, and the council will approve new funding only if this year's fuel tax revenue exceeds last year's. Since analysts expect this year's fuel tax revenue to fall short of last year's, the rail line will probably not be extended to Orland.
questions.stem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: The library will open a branch in Hartwell if the city donates land for it, and the city will donate the land if the zoning board approves the site. Since the zoning board is not expected to approve the site, the library probably will not open a branch in Hartwell.

The festival will be held downtown only if the city closes Main Street for it, and the city will close Main Street only if local merchants consent. Since the merchants are expected to refuse, the festival certainly will not be held downtown.

Only students who pass the qualifying exam may enroll in the seminar, and only students who finish the reading course pass the exam. Since most students who finish the reading course enroll in the seminar, most who pass the exam probably enroll as well.

The bridge will be repaired this year only if the state provides a grant, and the state will provide a grant only if the legislature passes a budget. Since the legislature is expected to pass a budget, the bridge will probably be repaired this year.

Since the club's membership is not likely to grow this year, the club probably will not hire a coach. After all, a coach will be hired only if dues revenue increases, and dues revenue will increase only if membership grows.
questions.explanation: The argument chains two necessary conditions (extension → funding → higher revenue), learns that the last condition probably fails, and concludes that the first event probably won't happen. (E) does exactly this, with the conclusion stated first. (B) is the trap: same chain, but it turns an expected failure into a certain one. (A) uses sufficient conditions, so denying the last one proves nothing; (D) affirms a necessary condition; and (C) has a different structure altogether.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The rail line will probably not be extended to Orland.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Extended → council funds; council funds → revenue exceeds last year's; revenue is expected to fall short.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: A only if B; B only if C; C probably fails; so A probably fails.

breakdown.analysis: Map it: Extend → Fund → Revenue up. The last link is expected to fail, so by the contrapositive the first is probably out. Check each answer for three things: two "only if" links in a chain, the last condition probably failing, and a conclusion hedged with "probably." Don't be thrown by order. The correct answer may put the conclusion first.

choices.note: Looks the same, but "if" isn't "only if." Donated land is enough for a branch, not required, so failing approval doesn't rule the branch out. Denying a sufficient condition is a different (flawed) pattern.
Tempting: the chain matches perfectly. But "expected to refuse" only makes failure likely, and it concludes "certainly." The original stays at "probably." One word, different reasoning.
Different structure. It reasons from a "most" statement about one group to another group, with no expected failure of a condition.
Affirms the necessary condition: a budget is required for the grant, not enough for it. The original denies a necessary condition. Opposite move.
CORRECT. Hire → dues up → membership grows; growth is unlikely; so probably no hire. Same chain, same hedge, conclusion moved to the front.

questions.stimulus: Ethicist: A software company recently found a flaw in its messaging app that could have let outsiders read file attachments. It fixed the flaw within a week but told no one, since nothing indicated that anyone had exploited it. This was wrong. Many clinics had used the app to send patients' medical records as attachments, and only the clinics could have alerted those patients.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the ethicist's argument?
choices: A company should disclose a security flaw only to people whose own information the flaw may have exposed, not to others who merely used the product.
A company that finds a flaw in its product should tell the product's users whenever the flaw may have exposed the personal information of those users themselves.
A company is not obligated to disclose a security flaw that it corrected before there was any evidence that the flaw had been exploited.
Anyone who learns that people's interests may have been put at risk ought to inform whoever is best placed to protect those people.
Those who send others' confidential information electronically are responsible for informing those others of any risk that it might be exposed.
questions.explanation: The ethicist condemns the company for silence even though no exploitation was known, because the clinics were the only ones who could warn the patients whose records were at stake. (D) generalizes exactly that: whoever learns of a possible risk to people should tell whoever can best protect them, here the clinics. (B) is the trap: it requires disclosure to users, but only when the users' own information was exposed, and the exposed information was the patients', not the clinics'. (A) would send the notice to the patients instead, (C) excuses the company, and (E) puts the duty on the clinics without saying the company did wrong.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The company acted wrongly in telling no one about the flaw.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The flaw could have exposed attachments; clinics had sent patients' medical records as attachments; only the clinics could have alerted the patients.

breakdown.analysis: Whose information was at risk? The patients'. Who did the company fail to tell? The clinics. So the principle can't be about telling people whose own data was exposed; it has to say you tell whoever can protect the people at risk. Notice too that the ethicist never disputes "no evidence of exploitation": the principle has to work on a mere possibility of risk. A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says, using the facts the argument actually gives.

choices.note: Points the wrong way. It would require telling the patients and rule out telling the clinics, who merely used the product. That doesn't make silence toward the clinics wrong; it doesn't even fit the ethicist's reason.

Tempting: users, a possible exposure, a duty to tell. But it covers only the users' own personal information. The records belonged to patients, so the condition isn't met and the principle doesn't reach this case. One word ("themselves") sinks it.
This is the company's defense. It clears the company.

CORRECT. The company learned that patients' interests may have been put at risk; the clinics were the only ones placed to protect them; so the company ought to have told the clinics, and staying silent was wrong.
Puts the duty on the clinics. Even if true, it says nothing about whether the company did wrong.

questions.stimulus: Most of the novels that one small press published last year were written by first-time novelists. And according to an industry survey, most first-time novelists whose books were published last year received advances of less than $5,000. So most of the novels the press published last year earned their authors advances of less than $5,000.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits a flawed pattern of reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?
choices: Most of the plants that the Hadley greenhouse sold last year were orchids. And according to a growers' survey, every orchid sold last year needed daily misting. So most of the plants Hadley sold last year needed daily misting.

Most of the paintings in the Ashcombe collection are by local artists. And according to a museum report, some paintings by local artists have been exhibited abroad. So some of the paintings in the Ashcombe collection have been exhibited abroad.
Most applicants to the Velor fellowship are from the town of Varn, and most of the fellowship's recipients are from Varn as well. So most applicants from Varn end up receiving the fellowship.

More than half of the cars Dunmore Motors sold last month were electric, and a majority of electric cars sold in the region last month were priced above $40,000. Hence, most of Dunmore's sales last month were of cars priced above $40,000.

Most members of the Orrin hiking club are retirees. And according to a regional survey, most retirees in the region hike at least once a week. So at least some members of the Orrin hiking club hike at least once a week.
questions.explanation: The argument says most of group A (the press's novels) are B (by first-timers), and most of all B get C (small advances), then concludes most of A get C. That fails, because the press's first-timers could be among the minority who got larger advances. (D) has the same two "most" premises and the same "most" conclusion, with the premises in reverse order. (E) is the trap: it shares the flawed overlap but concludes only "at least some," a different conclusion. (A) is a valid version ("every orchid"), (B) moves from "some" to "some," and (C) reverses the relationship between groups.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Most of one small press's novels last year earned advances under $5,000.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most the press novels were by first-time novelists; most first-time novelists published last year got advances under $5,000.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Most A are B; most B (in general) are C; so most A are C.

breakdown.analysis: Is that safe? No. "Most first-timers" covers the whole industry. the press's first-timers could be the lucky few with big advances. Picture 100 first-time novelists, 70 with small advances; the press published 10 of the other 30. The match has to keep both "most" premises, the broader second group, and a "most" conclusion. Check the conclusion's quantifier last; that's where the trap hides. Also cross off any valid answer: a parallel-flaw answer must be flawed.

choices.note: Valid. "Every orchid" means every Hadley orchid needed misting, so the conclusion follows. The original is flawed, so this can't match.
Flawed, but differently. It mixes "most" and "some" and concludes "some." The original uses "most" throughout.
Different error. It flips the relationship: from "most recipients are from Varn" it infers that most people from Varn are recipients.

CORRECT. Strip the vocabulary: most of Dunmore's cars were electric ("more than half"); most electric cars in the region, a broader group, cost over $40,000 ("a majority"); so most of Dunmore's cars did. Same gap: Dunmore's electrics could be the cheap ones. The synonyms and the swapped premise order are what hide the match.

Tempting: the flaw is the same overlap, and the wording mirrors the original almost line for line. But it concludes "at least some," not "most." A parallel answer has to match the conclusion's strength, and this one doesn't.

questions.stimulus: Apartment rents in downtown Ferrisport have risen 30 percent in just three years, and the share of downtown apartments standing vacant is the lowest in decades. Meanwhile, many downtown office buildings stand largely empty, and their owners are eager to sell. So a developer who bought these office buildings and converted them into apartments would find the investment highly profitable.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Apartment rents in Ferrisport's suburbs have risen far less over the past three years than rents downtown have.
Over the past decade, Ferrisport's downtown population has grown considerably faster than the city's supply of downtown housing has.
Developers in Ferrisport have generally earned higher returns from building new apartment complexes than from converting existing buildings.
The downtown units whose rents have climbed nearly all have windows in every room, which the offices' deep floor plans cannot provide.
Many of the office tenants who have left downtown Ferrisport moved to newer and cheaper office space in the suburbs.
questions.explanation: The argument assumes that converted offices would earn the rents downtown apartments now command. (D) shows the rent surge is for a kind of unit the office buildings cannot become, so converted units may not share in it. (C) is the trap: it says conversion earns less than new construction, but a comparison with another investment does not show that conversion would not be highly profitable. (B) strengthens, and (A) and (E) do not bear on converted units' rents.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Converting the empty downtown office buildings into apartments would be highly profitable.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Downtown rents are up 30 percent in three years and vacancy is at a decades low; many office buildings are empty and for sale.

breakdown.analysis: The argument treats 'downtown apartments' as one market. Would the converted units actually get those rents? Only if they're the kind of apartment renters are paying up for. It's like seeing that three-bedroom houses are selling fast and concluding your studio will too. We need an answer that shows converted offices wouldn't share in the rent boom. Most students pick (C) because 'lower returns' sounds like 'not profitable.' It fails because it's a comparison: conversion can earn less than new construction and still be highly profitable. Watch the switch from a relative claim (less profitable than) to an absolute one (highly profitable). (D) looks like a detail about windows until you see it splits the market.

choices.note: Wrong. Suburban rents aren't the issue. The conversions would be downtown, where rents are high.
Wrong. This strengthens the case: demand outpacing supply supports high rents for new units.

Tempting. It sounds like conversion is a worse deal. But 'less profitable than new construction' doesn't mean 'not highly profitable.' Both could be lucrative. A relative claim can't sink an absolute one.
CORRECT. The rent boom is in units with windows in every room. Deep office floor plans can't give that, so converted units would be outside the hot segment and may not command the high rents.
Wrong. This explains why the offices are empty. It says nothing about what converted apartments would earn.

questions.stimulus: Climatologist: Of the severe storms that struck one stretch of coast over the past decade, 70 percent were preceded by a week of unusually warm temperatures in the adjacent sea. Records of sea temperatures and storms for that decade are complete and reliable. Hence, whenever the sea off that coast has a week of unusually warm temperatures, a severe storm will probably follow.
questions.stem: The climatologist's argument is flawed because it
choices: treats a correlation between two kinds of events as proof that one causes the other
infers how often one kind of event follows another from how often the second was preceded by the first
fails to consider that some of the severe storms struck the coast after weeks of entirely normal sea temperatures
presumes, without providing justification, that unusually warm seas are the only factor that can produce a severe storm
fails to consider how many severe storms struck the coast over the decade covered by the records
questions.explanation: The premise starts from storms and looks back (70 percent of storms followed a warm week); the conclusion starts from warm weeks and looks forward (a warm week will probably bring a storm). (B) describes that reversal abstractly. (E) is the near-miss: it points at a missing number, but the wrong one; however many storms there were, what decides the conclusion is how many warm weeks there were. (A) names the textbook causal flaw, but the conclusion is a prediction, not a causal claim; (C) is conceded by the 70 percent figure; and (D) is a claim the argument never makes.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Whenever the sea has an unusually warm week, a severe storm will probably follow.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 70 percent of the decade's severe storms came after an unusually warm week; the records are complete and reliable.

breakdown.analysis: Most storms had a warm week first. Does that mean most warm weeks bring a storm? Quick numbers: 10 storms, 7 after warm weeks, but 50 warm weeks in the decade. Only 7 of 50 warm weeks led to a storm. The missing number is how many warm weeks there were. It's like: most lottery winners bought a ticket that week, so if you buy a ticket you'll probably win. Most students go for (A) because correlation-versus-causation is the flaw everyone knows, or for (E) because it spots that a count is missing. (E) asks for the wrong count. (B) is hard to like because it's so abstract: read it slowly and it describes exactly the storms-to-warm-weeks flip.

choices.note: Tempting. It's the classic flaw. But the climatologist never says warm water causes storms; the conclusion is that a storm will probably follow. The error is in the proportions, not a causal leap.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Cities with more libraries have lower crime, so building libraries causes crime to fall.

choices.note: CORRECT. The "second kind" is storms, the "first kind" is warm weeks. From how often storms were preceded by warm weeks (70 percent), the argument infers how likely warm weeks are to be followed by storms. Those are different fractions.
Already conceded. The 70 percent figure leaves 30 percent of storms without a warm week, and the argument doesn't hide it.
The argument never says warm seas are the only cause. It openly allows that 30 percent of storms came without them.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Smoking causes lung disease, so anyone with lung disease must have smoked.

choices.note: The near-miss. Right instinct (a count is missing), wrong count. With 10 storms or 100, the conclusion still depends on how many warm weeks there were. Knowing the number of storms alone can't tell you what share of warm weeks led to one.

questions.stimulus: Over the past five years, the Corvell Courier has lost half of its readers under the age of thirty. During the same period, young people have increasingly gotten their news from short online videos rather than from newspapers. So if the Courier begins producing short news videos of its own, it will win back many of the young readers it has lost.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
choices: Producing short news videos is the only way for the Courier to win back any of its lost young readers.
All of the young readers the Courier lost stopped reading it because they began getting their news from short videos instead.
At least some of the young readers the Courier lost still seek out the kind of news that the Courier reports.
Producing short news videos will not cost the Courier more than it can afford to spend on new projects.
Short news videos produced by the Courier would be at least as popular with young people as those of its competitors.
questions.explanation: To win back lost young readers with its own videos, the Courier needs at least some of those readers still to want the kind of news it covers. If none of them do, videos in a new format won't bring them back: (C). (B) is the trap: it is the story the evidence suggests, but it says "all," and the argument survives if only some readers left for that reason. (A) and (E) are too strong, and (D) addresses whether the plan is affordable, which the conditional conclusion does not depend on.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: If the Courier produces short news videos, it will win back many of the young readers it lost.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The Courier lost half its readers under thirty in five years; over that time young people increasingly got their news from short online videos.

breakdown.analysis: Change the format and they'll come back? Only if they still want what the Courier offers. If those readers have lost interest in that kind of news altogether, no video will lure them. It's like a bakery that lost customers to delivery apps and expects delivery to win them back: that only works if they still want bread. We need a modest answer that says at least some of the lost readers still want this kind of news. Most students pick (B) because it's the obvious reason they left. Negate it, though, and the argument survives.

choices.note: Too strong. Negated (there are other ways too), videos could still win readers back.
choices.negation: Producing short news videos is not the only way for the Courier to win back young readers.

choices.note: Tempting: it's the story the premises hint at. But "all" is far more than the argument needs. Negate it (not all of them left for that reason) and the argument is untouched: winning back many of them needs only that some left for videos, or will watch videos now.
choices.negation: Not all of the young readers the Courier lost stopped reading it because they began getting their news from short videos.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: none of the lost readers seek out the Courier's kind of news anymore. Then Courier videos have nothing to win them back with, and the conclusion collapses.
choices.negation: None of the young readers the Courier has lost still seek out news of the kind that the Courier reports.

choices.note: The conclusion is conditional: if the Courier makes videos, readers return. Whether it can afford them is a separate question. Negated, the conditional still stands.
choices.negation: Producing short news videos will cost the Courier more than it can afford to spend on new projects.
