choices.note: Too strong. The Courier needs to win back many of its own lost readers, not beat its competitors. Negated, it could still succeed.
choices.negation: The Courier's short news videos would be less popular with young people than its competitors' videos.

passages.title: The Venice Charter and Its Critics
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
Since the Venice Charter of 1964, the prevailing principle in conserving historic buildings has been that new work should declare itself. The Charter’s twelfth article requires that replacements of missing parts “integrate harmoniously with the whole” but remain “distinguishable from the original so that restoration does not falsify the artistic or historic evidence.” A conservator who follows the principle sets new stone in a slightly different tone or leaves new moldings plain, so that visitors can tell old from new. Behind the rule lies an analogy: a building stands to its public much as a document stands to its readers, so a repair’s first duty is not to falsify the record. Imitative repair, which reproduces lost parts in their original manner, thus passes off the work of one age as the testimony of another.

The principle has drawn two practical objections. Few buildings reach us in a single state, and critics ask which state the rule protects. Consider a parish church whose medieval nave received a new west front in the 1720s and a new roof in the 1860s, and which was gutted by fire in wartime and repaired in the 1950s with stone of a cooler gray. The 1950s work is set off against all earlier fabric alike, as though the eighteenth-century front were as original as the nave; the seam it creates is one cut among many, singled out chiefly because it is the latest. Critics note, too, that a contrast need not stay visible: stone weathers, and a repair meant to be legible may within a generation match its surroundings so closely that only a guidebook can locate it.

A deeper objection came from outside the European tradition that produced the Charter. The principal sanctuaries of the Ise Grand Shrine in Japan have been rebuilt in the same form, with one long interruption, at intervals of roughly twenty years for well over a millennium. To demand that each rebuilding look different, critics argue, would mistake what is being preserved, which is a practice of making rather than a particular set of timbers. On this view a farmer who replaces a barn’s rotted boards with identical ones is maintaining a tool, not tampering with a record, and a conspicuous seam can itself mislead, suggesting a catastrophe where there was only routine upkeep.

The Nara Document on Authenticity (1994), framed partly in answer to such objections, did not repudiate the Charter; it presented itself as building on the Charter’s spirit. But by holding that authenticity must be judged within a building’s own cultural context, it changed what the Charter’s rule demands in practice. A conservator must now decide what a building is—document, instrument, or continuing practice—before knowing whether a matching repair falsifies anything, and only for a document does a visible seam follow directly.

passages.title: Participatory Budgeting
passages.subject: social-science
passages.text:
Participatory budgeting—the practice of letting residents vote directly on how a portion of a city’s capital budget will be spent—has spread to thousands of cities since Porto Alegre, Brazil, adopted it in 1989, and its advocates present it as a remedy for civic disengagement. Its critics raise three objections. First, those who take part are not a fair sample of the city: the meetings at which residents decide which proposals will reach the ballot are typically held on weeknight evenings, and they favor residents with flexible schedules, reliable child care, and the confidence to speak in public. Second, the process is biased toward the visible. Residents predictably prefer new playgrounds, murals, and bike lanes—things they can point to—over replacing aging water mains, so a city that budgets this way may starve its least glamorous infrastructure. Third, the process blurs accountability: when a poorly chosen project fails, council members can say that residents chose it, and residents chose it as a crowd.

The record of one midsized North American city, which in 2014 began setting aside 2 percent of its capital budget for residents to allocate, bears on the first two. Local skeptics predicted that the process would be captured by the handful of activists who dominate every public hearing. Yet because the city accepted ballots by mail and at libraries and grocery stores over a two-week period, residents of its lowest-income neighborhoods have cast a larger share of the votes than their share of the city’s population in each of the program’s first eight cycles. Nor has the program crowded out ordinary obligations: residents decide only how the set-aside is spent, and the remaining 98 percent of the capital budget, including every dollar for water and sewer systems, is still allocated by the council. And residents’ choices have often addressed problems that the city’s engineers had missed—a dangerous pedestrian crossing near a senior center, for instance, that had never appeared in a traffic study because no one had yet been killed there.

The first two objections, this experience suggests, describe features of particular programs that can be designed away, not flaws inherent in the practice. The third stands; nothing in the city’s arrangements makes it easier to say who answers for a project that fails. The experience also points to a benefit the critics overlook. Residents who have spent weeks weighing a new streetlight against a repaired sidewalk come away with a far clearer sense of the trade-offs every budget involves. Officials who dismiss such programs as symbolic because they control only a sliver of the budget are measuring them by the size of the sums at stake, when their chief return lies in what residents learn by deciding how to spend them.

passages.title: The Texas Rolling Beach Easement
passages.subject: law
passages.text:
Under the Texas Open Beaches Act of 1959, the public may use the dry-sand beach along the Gulf of Mexico—roughly, the strip between the water’s edge and the line of vegetation—wherever it has acquired a right to that sand, as by long use or an owner’s dedication, even within privately titled lots. But much of the Texas shore is retreating. When erosion pushes the vegetation line inland, does the easement move with it onto former lawns and house lots, or stay fixed and vanish into the sea?

A fixed easement respects private titles but lets the public beach vanish; a rolling one keeps the beach public but shifts public use onto land its owners never surrendered. In Severance v. Patterson, a dispute arising after Hurricane Rita shifted the vegetation line on Galveston Island, the Texas Supreme Court, in its 2012 opinion on rehearing, took a middle course drawn from the older law of boundaries along water. It distinguished erosion, a gradual and imperceptible loss of land, from avulsion, a sudden and perceptible one of the kind a hurricane causes. The easement follows gradual change, so a beach that creeps inland carries the public’s right with it. When a storm abruptly strips away the dunes, however, the easement does not migrate onto the newly exposed sand, and the state must establish the public’s right to that sand anew. Thus an owner whose dune line retreated thirty meters in one hurricane could exclude the public from the exposed sand, whereas a neighbor who lost the same thirty meters over twenty years could not.

The compromise, however, rests on a distinction that fits beaches poorly. Coastal scientists note that much apparently gradual retreat is the cumulative work of many small storms, while a single storm’s losses are often partly reversed as sand returns in later months. A court applying the rule must therefore decide how quickly a line moved, a question the physical record often cannot answer. And on a storm-battered coast, as public access advocates have warned, the exception for sudden change threatens to become the rule.

The property scholar Helen Corwin has proposed a different test. A court would ask only whether a shift in the vegetation line had persisted for a fixed period—she suggests five years. If it had, the easement would move to the new line however the shift occurred; if the line returned seaward within that period, nothing would change. Corwin concedes that any such period is arbitrary at the margin, but the test’s chief merit is evidentiary: it would ask courts to determine where a line has stood rather than to reconstruct how quickly it got there. That merit should be decisive: courts would do better to adopt some test of persistence than to keep asking how fast the sand moved.

passages.title: Dark Eggs in Cold Climates
passages.subject: natural-science
passages.text:
Birds’ eggs are often colored for concealment, and for species that nest on open ground the logic seems clear: eggs that match the surrounding sand or gravel are found by predators less often than eggs that do not, as experiments with artificial clutches show. Yet a survey of eggshell color across more than six hundred bird species, published in 2020, found that eggs laid in colder regions tend to be darker and browner than those laid in warmer ones, although against the pale gravels of many high-latitude nesting grounds darker eggs should be easier to find. The survey’s authors proposed that the pattern reflects a need for warmth, and their experiments showed that darker shells warm faster in sunlight.

The ecologist Lena Varga has argued that the warmth explanation holds with special force for some ground-nesting shorebirds. In some such species only one parent incubates, and, unfed by its mate, it must leave the nest repeatedly each day to forage. While it is away the eggs cool, and an embryo whose temperature falls below roughly 26°C stops developing until it is warmed again. Wind hastens that cooling much as cold air does. Each pause lengthens incubation, and every extra day in the nest is a day on which the clutch can be lost. Dark shells absorb more sunlight than pale ones and so slow the eggs’ cooling; where the air is cold, Varga contends, that gain outweighs the loss of camouflage.

At a subarctic colony of one sandpiper species in which the female alone incubates, air temperatures during incubation averaged 8°C and foraging trips about 25 minutes. A pale egg left in sunlight cooled from 36°C to the threshold in about 15 minutes, so on a typical trip its embryo spent some 10 minutes with development halted; over the 150 or so trips of a full incubation, those pauses came to about 25 hours. A dark egg under the same conditions took about 28 minutes to reach the threshold. At a colony of the same species near the southern edge of its range, where females’ trips were no longer than in the north and incubation-season air averaged near 20°C, even pale eggs took more than an hour to cool that far.

Comparisons within the species point the same way. An exposed, wind-scoured island colony lays markedly darker eggs than a sheltered valley colony at the same latitude. And in the northern colonies, darker clutches hatched more often overall than paler ones, even though predators found them somewhat more often day for day. A decisive test is within reach: exchange clutches between the palest- and darkest-laying females of one northern colony. If hatching success follows the eggs, the shell itself confers the advantage; if it follows the females, some trait of theirs, such as briefer foraging, does.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Because new stone weathers to match old stone within a generation, the requirement that repairs be distinguishable cannot be satisfied for long in most historic buildings.
The rebuilding of the Ise Grand Shrine shows that faithful reproduction, rather than visible contrast, is the only honest way to conserve wooden buildings.
Since few historic buildings survive in a single state, conservators should treat all of a building’s fabric, whatever its date, as equally original.
Although the rule that repairs be visibly set apart from older fabric remains useful for some buildings, the Nara Document has largely replaced it with a preference for faithful reproduction.
The rule that repairs stand apart from older fabric treats buildings as records, and objections to it have made its use depend on first deciding what a building is.
questions.explanation: The passage sets out the Venice Charter’s rule and its record-keeping rationale (first paragraph), reports practical and more fundamental objections (second and third), and ends by saying that after Nara a conservator must first decide what a building is before the rule’s demand follows. E summarizes that arc in other words. D is the near-miss: it carries the same kind of hedging (“remains useful for some buildings,” “largely”), but the passage says Nara built on the Charter rather than replacing it, and never says Nara prefers reproduction. A promotes one objection to the thesis, B overgeneralizes the Ise example, and C recommends a position no one in the passage takes.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Main point: what does the passage as a whole establish?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Whole passage; the last paragraph says where the account ends up.

breakdown.analysis: Map it: the rule and why it exists (records shouldn’t be falsified) → two practical objections → a deeper objection from Ise → Nara, which keeps the Charter but makes authenticity depend on cultural context, so the rule now applies only once you know what kind of thing the building is. Prephrase: “The Charter’s visible-repair rule, built on the building-as-record idea, has been challenged, and now its use depends on first deciding what a building is.” Both D and E are carefully hedged, so don’t pick on hedges; pick on what the last paragraph actually says about Nara.

choices.note: Too narrow and too strong. Weathering is one of the practical objections in the second paragraph, and the critics say a repair “may” come to match, not that it always does.
Overgeneralizes. Ise is offered as a case where reproduction is continuity, not as proof that reproduction is the only honest method for all wooden buildings.
Too strong. The parish church shows that the rule singles out the latest layer, but no one in the passage tells conservators to treat every layer as equally original.

Tempting, because it is hedged the way a good main-point answer is. But the last paragraph says Nara “did not repudiate” the Charter and presented itself as building on it; it changed how the rule is applied, not replaced it with a preference for reproduction.

CORRECT. “Stand apart from older fabric” = distinguishable; “treats buildings as records” = the document analogy; “objections … have made its use depend on first deciding what a building is” = the last paragraph’s point about Nara.

questions.stem: The author’s attitude toward the principle described in the first paragraph can most accurately be described as
choices: rejection of it as a doctrine that has on balance done more harm than good to historic buildings
evenhanded exposition of both its rationale and the objections to it, neither endorsing nor dismissing it
approval of its aims, tempered by regret that conservators have applied it carelessly in particular cases
skepticism grounded in the view that the Nara Document has rendered it obsolete
admiration for its consistency, qualified by concern that it is costly and difficult to carry out
questions.explanation: The author explains the rule’s rationale (the document analogy) and attributes every objection to critics (“critics ask,” “critics note,” “critics argue”), then reports how Nara changed the rule’s application without saying the rule is right or wrong. That is B. D is the near-miss: Nara does limit the rule’s reach, but the author says Nara built on the Charter rather than making it obsolete. A overshoots, C invents careless application, and E invents a concern about cost.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Attitude: how does the author stand toward the distinguishability rule?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Who voices each objection (second and third paragraphs) and how the fourth paragraph describes Nara.

breakdown.analysis: Whose objections are these? Look at the tags: “critics ask,” “critics note,” “critics argue,” “on this view.” The author reports them. The rule’s rationale is laid out just as fairly in the first paragraph. Even the last paragraph describes what Nara did to the rule rather than grading the rule. So the attitude is descriptive and balanced. Attitude answers come in two halves; check that the author really holds both.

choices.note: Too strong. The author never weighs harm against good and never rejects the rule; the objections belong to critics.
CORRECT. The rationale (first paragraph) and the objections (second and third) are both set out, the objections are attributed to critics, and the author neither defends nor discards the rule.
Invents a complaint. Nothing in the passage says conservators applied the rule carelessly; the parish church was repaired exactly as the rule directs.
Tempting, since Nara narrows where the rule applies. But the passage says Nara “did not repudiate” the Charter and built on it, so “obsolete” misstates both Nara and the author.
Cost is never mentioned, and the author doesn’t praise the rule’s consistency.

questions.stem: The author discusses the parish church in the second paragraph primarily in order to
choices: give an example of a repair carried out in violation of the principle that new work should be distinguishable from the old fabric around it
show that contrasting new stone of the kind used at the church eventually comes to resemble the older stone around it
suggest that eighteenth-century additions to a building ought to be regarded by conservators as part of its original fabric
show that in a building altered over several periods, the rule sets apart only the newest intervention, letting older ones pass as original
argue that buildings altered in several different periods should be repaired by imitating their earliest surviving form
questions.explanation: The paragraph raises the question of which state the rule protects and uses the church, with its medieval nave, 1720s front, 1860s roof, and 1950s repair, to show that the repair contrasts with all earlier fabric alike, so earlier alterations count as “original.” D says this in different words. B is the near-miss: weathering appears later in the same paragraph, but it is a separate objection, and the church is not used to illustrate it. A reverses the case (the repair follows the rule), and C and E draw recommendations no one makes.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Function: why is the parish church in the passage?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, especially its first and last sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Read the sentence before the example: critics ask “which state the rule protects.” The church has four layers, and the 1950s repair is set off against all the others “as though the eighteenth-century front were as original as the nave.” So the example shows that the rule flags only the newest layer and treats every older one as original. Prephrase: “to show that the rule marks off only the latest change in a many-layered building.”

choices.note: Backward. The 1950s repair follows the principle; that’s the point. The trouble is what following it does.

Tempting, because the church’s stone is “a cooler gray” and weathering comes up later in the same paragraph. But weathering is a separate objection (“Critics note, too”), and the church example is about which layer gets treated as new.
The passage notes that the repair treats the eighteenth-century front as original, as a criticism of the rule’s logic. It doesn’t say the front ought to be regarded that way.

CORRECT. “Sets apart only the newest intervention” = the 1950s seam, “singled out chiefly because it is the latest”; “letting older ones pass as original” = treating the 1720s front “as original as the nave.”
No repair method is recommended here, least of all imitating a building’s earliest form.

questions.stem: The passage raises each of the following as a difficulty for the principle that new work should be distinguishable from old EXCEPT:
choices: the tendency of contrasting new material to come to resemble the surrounding material over time
the existence of traditions in which reproducing a structure faithfully is a way of keeping it alive
a conflict between making replacements distinguishable and making them fit harmoniously with the whole
the possibility that a conspicuous seam will lead viewers to infer an event that never took place
the presence in many buildings of alterations made in several different periods
questions.explanation: Four choices match difficulties the passage raises: weathering (A, second paragraph), Ise (B, third), a seam suggesting a catastrophe (D, third), and buildings that reach us in several states (E, second). The Charter’s demand that replacements “integrate harmoniously with the whole” is quoted in the first paragraph, but the passage never treats it as being in tension with distinguishability, so C is the exception. C is hard to spot because its language does come from the passage.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: EXCEPT: four choices are difficulties the passage raises for the principle; find the one it doesn’t raise.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph (layers, weathering), third (Ise, barns, misleading seams). The first paragraph quotes the Charter.

breakdown.analysis: Check each choice against the list of objections. The trick here is that the odd one out isn’t foreign to the passage. “Integrate harmoniously” really is in the first paragraph, so a skimmer ticks it off as “mentioned.” But mentioned isn’t the same as raised as a difficulty. The passage quotes that phrase only to describe the Charter and never sets the two demands against each other. The lesson: in an EXCEPT item, check what role the text gives a detail, not just whether the detail appears.

choices.note: Raised in the second paragraph: a repair meant to be legible may come to match its surroundings.
Raised in the third paragraph: Ise is rebuilt in the same form to preserve “a practice of making.”
CORRECT. The “harmoniously” requirement is quoted in the first paragraph, but the passage never says it conflicts with distinguishability. It is mentioned, not raised as a difficulty.
Raised in the third paragraph: a seam can suggest “a catastrophe where there was only routine upkeep.”
Raised in the second paragraph: “Few buildings reach us in a single state.”

questions.stem: The passage suggests that if the principle described in the first paragraph were applied to future work on the parish church in the same way it was applied after the fire, any new repair would have to be
choices: set visibly apart from the stone installed in the 1950s no less than from the fabric that preceded it
designed so that visitors could tell the eighteenth-century west front apart from the medieval nave
matched to the cooler gray of the 1950s stone, so that all work done under the principle reads as one layer
made to contrast with the church’s earliest surviving fabric, but not with any of the later additions
confined to those parts of the church that were not altered in either the 1720s or the 1860s
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says the 1950s repair was set off against all earlier fabric alike, so the rule as applied treats whatever already exists as “the original.” A future repair applied the same way would treat the 1950s stone as existing fabric and set itself off from it too, which is A. B is the dominant trap: telling the 1720s front from the nave is what the critics’ complaint points toward, not what the rule as applied does. D reverses the rule’s practice, and C and E have no basis in the passage.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Inference: project the rule, as it was actually applied to the church, onto the next repair.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph (how the 1950s repair was set off), with the rule in the first paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: How did the 1950s repair decide what counts as “old”? It set itself off “against all earlier fabric alike.” So the rule, as applied, treats everything already there as original. Run the clock forward: next time, the 1950s stone is already there, so the new work must be set off from it too. That’s a commitment the passage never states. Most students pick (B), because the critics complain that the 1720s front was lumped in with the nave. But that’s the critics’ objection to the rule, not what the rule does. The stem asks how the rule works when applied the same way again.

choices.note: CORRECT. Applied as it was after the fire, the rule sets new work off from everything already there, and the 1950s stone will be part of what is already there.
Tempting. This is the trap. Distinguishing the 1720s front from the nave is what the critics’ complaint points toward; the rule as applied lumped them together.
Backward. The rule demands that new work be distinguishable; matching the 1950s stone would hide the new repair against it.
Reverses the practice the passage describes. The 1950s work contrasted with all earlier fabric, later additions included, not just the oldest layer.
Nothing in the passage limits repairs to unaltered parts of a building.

questions.stem: The critics whose objections are described in the passage would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: A repair carried out according to a local tradition of faithful reproduction cannot misrepresent the history of the building it restores.
Conservators ought to abandon the requirement of distinguishability in favor of imitative repair wherever a building is still in use.
Making a repair conspicuous does not by itself guarantee that the repair conveys an accurate account of a building’s past.
How a building ought to be repaired is a more basic question than what kind of thing the building is.
A repair that has weathered to match its surroundings no longer makes any claim about the building’s past.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph reports the critics’ view that “a conspicuous seam can itself mislead, suggesting a catastrophe where there was only routine upkeep.” So visibility alone does not ensure an accurate account, which is C. E borrows the weathering objection but adds a conclusion the critics never draw; a matched repair becomes hard to locate, not claim-free. A overstates the Ise point, B prescribes a policy no one endorses, and D reverses the order of the two questions the passage raises.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Other party’s view: which statement would the critics accept?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, especially “a conspicuous seam can itself mislead,” and the second paragraph’s objections.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase, so test each choice against a specific line. The critics’ sharpest point is that the very thing the rule demands, a visible seam, can itself mislead. So conspicuousness isn’t a guarantee of honesty. Watch for answers that take a tradition the critics defend and turn it into a rule that can never fail.

choices.note: Too strong. The critics say Ise’s rebuilding isn’t deceit given what is being preserved, but “cannot misrepresent” any history goes far beyond that.
No one in the passage recommends abandoning the rule, and “still in use” is a test nobody proposes; the barn is one case.
CORRECT. A conspicuous seam “can itself mislead,” so being visible doesn’t ensure that a repair tells the truth about the past.
Backward. The passage makes what a building is the prior question, to be settled before deciding how a repair should look.
Tempting, because weathering really is one of the critics’ objections. But they say the repair becomes hard to locate, not that it stops making a claim.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: argue that a city can protect its least glamorous infrastructure only by leaving all spending on water and sewer systems to its council
show that participatory budgeting has failed to remedy civic disengagement because its agenda-setting meetings favor residents with flexible schedules
use one city’s record to argue that some criticisms of a practice can be designed away and that it has a neglected benefit
argue that because participatory budgeting controls only a small share of a city’s budget, its value is educational rather than financial
defend participatory budgeting against each of the principal objections its critics have raised, relying on the experience of a single city
questions.explanation: The passage sets out three objections, uses one city’s experience to argue that the first two can be designed away, grants that the third remains, and adds a benefit the critics overlook. C says this with the passage’s own limits (“some criticisms”). E is the near-miss: the author explicitly concedes that the third objection, about accountability, is not answered. A and D overstate single points, and B contradicts the turnout evidence.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Primary purpose: what is the passage as a whole trying to do?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Whole passage, especially the first two sentences of the third paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Three objections, one city, a split verdict, and a bonus benefit. So the purpose is a qualified defense, not a full one. Prephrase: “use a city’s experience to show that two criticisms can be designed around, while adding a benefit critics miss.” Watch for the answer that claims all three objections are met: the author says “The third is another matter.”

choices.note: Too strong. Leaving water and sewer to the council is how this city avoided the problem; the passage never says it is the only way.
Contradicts the passage. In this city the lowest-income neighborhoods were overrepresented among voters.
CORRECT. One city’s record, two criticisms met by design (“some”), and the learning benefit critics overlook.
Mangles the last sentence. The author faults officials for judging programs by sums spent, but doesn’t say their value is only educational or that this follows from their size.
Tempting, since the passage is mostly favorable. But the author concedes that the third objection (accountability) is not answered.

questions.stem: According to the passage, critics contend that residents choosing among proposed projects tend to favor projects that
choices: serve the interests of residents who have the time and confidence to attend proposal meetings
produce results whose benefits are apparent to residents rather than hidden from them
improve the appearance of a neighborhood rather than the safety of its residents
correct hazards that the city’s engineers have overlooked in their traffic studies
cost little to maintain once they have been built
questions.explanation: The second objection says the process is “biased toward the visible”: residents prefer things “they can point to” over replacing hidden water mains. B restates that. A is drawn from the first objection, which concerns who attends meetings, not which projects are favored. C is the near-miss: murals and playgrounds might suggest appearance, but bike lanes are on the list too, and the critics’ contrast is with buried infrastructure, not with safety. D is the author’s point, not the critics’.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Detail: what kind of project do critics say residents prefer?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First paragraph, the second objection.

breakdown.analysis: The critics’ contrast is visible versus invisible: playgrounds, murals, bike lanes on one side; aging water mains on the other. Prephrase: “things you can see.” Two answers borrow from nearby text: one from the first objection, one from the author’s rebuttal.

choices.note: Wrong objection. The first objection is about who takes part in the meetings, not what kind of project voters prefer.
CORRECT. “Biased toward the visible” and “things they can point to” versus buried water mains: benefits residents can see versus ones hidden from them.
Tempting, because murals and playgrounds look cosmetic. But bike lanes are on the list, and the critics’ contrast is with unseen infrastructure, not with safety.
Wrong party. That is the author’s point about the city’s results (the pedestrian crossing), not a critics’ claim.
Not stated. The critics say nothing about maintenance costs.

questions.stem: The author mentions the pedestrian crossing near a senior center (last sentence of the second paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: give an example of a highly visible project of the kind that critics say residents tend to favor over infrastructure
suggest that the city’s engineers are, on the whole, less competent than residents at identifying hazards
illustrate the benefit that the author says the critics of participatory budgeting have overlooked
indicate that residents generally prefer projects that improve safety to projects that merely improve a neighborhood’s appearance
show that residents may know of local problems that the city’s usual ways of identifying problems fail to register
questions.explanation: The crossing never appeared in a traffic study “because no one had yet been killed there,” yet residents chose to fix it: residents knew something the city’s formal methods missed. E says this abstractly. C is the strongest trap: the third paragraph does name a benefit the critics overlook, but that benefit is what residents learn about budget trade-offs, not the problems they spot. B and D overgeneralize from one case, and A misreads the crossing as the kind of showy project critics complain about.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Function: why mention the crossing near the senior center?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, last sentence; compare the third paragraph’s “benefit the critics overlook.”

breakdown.analysis: Why hadn’t the city’s engineers flagged the crossing? Their traffic studies count accidents, and there hadn’t been one yet. Residents knew better. So the example shows residents adding local knowledge that the city’s methods don’t catch. The tempting wrong answer ties it to the “overlooked benefit” in the next paragraph. Read that paragraph again: the benefit is what residents learn by weighing costs, a different point.

choices.note: Backward. The crossing is a safety fix the experts had missed, not the playground-and-mural kind of project critics complain about.
Too strong. One missed crossing doesn’t show engineers are generally less competent, and the passage explains the miss by how traffic studies work.
Tempting. This is the trap. The overlooked benefit in the third paragraph is what residents learn about trade-offs, not the hazards they identify.
Overgeneralizes from a single case; the passage never compares residents’ general preferences for safety and appearance.
CORRECT. The crossing never showed up in a traffic study because no one had been killed there; residents’ local knowledge caught what the city’s methods missed.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to the error the author attributes to the officials mentioned in the last sentence of the passage?
choices: faulting a museum for spending only a small share of its budget on educational programs that attract few visitors
judging a small grant program by how many applicants it attracts rather than by how much money it distributes
criticizing a training course for teaching skills that its participants could have learned on the job at no cost
evaluating a town meeting by the number of residents it draws rather than by the decisions it reaches
calling a volunteer mentoring program trivial because no wages change hands, when what participants gain from it is a skill
questions.explanation: The officials judge the programs by the size of the sums at stake, when their chief return is what participants learn. E matches both elements: the mentoring program is judged by money when its value lies in the skill gained. B reverses the error (it recommends judging by money), D swaps in a different wrong measure (attendance) and a different true one (decisions), and C mentions learning but describes a different complaint. A concerns a budget share but not a mistaken yardstick.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Analogy: find the situation with the same mistake the officials make.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: What exactly is the officials’ error? Two parts: 1. they measure the program by how much money is involved; 2. the program’s real payoff is what the participants learn. The right answer needs both: something judged by its dollars when it’s really for teaching. Analogy answers that match one element and not the other are the standard trap.

choices.note: Mentions budget shares and education, but the complaint here is about low attendance, not about using money as the yardstick for something whose value is learning.
Backward. This says money distributed is the right measure, which is the officials’ mistake turned into advice.
Tempting, because it involves learning. But the criticism is that the lessons were available free elsewhere, not that the course was judged by the money involved.
Has the “wrong yardstick” shape, but neither element matches: attendance isn’t money, and decisions aren’t participants’ learning.
CORRECT. Judged by money (“no wages change hands”) when what it really delivers is learning (a skill). Both elements match.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which one of the following was true of the city’s program during its first eight cycles?
choices: Proposal meetings were moved from weeknight evenings to times more convenient for working residents.
Most of the votes were cast by residents who had never before attended a public hearing on the budget.
Residents were permitted to allocate part of the set-aside to the repair of water and sewer systems.
Residents of the poorest neighborhoods were overrepresented among those who voted.
The activists who dominate the city’s public hearings cast a smaller share of the votes than their share of the population.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says residents of the lowest-income neighborhoods “cast a larger share of the votes than their share of the city’s population in each of the program’s first eight cycles,” which D paraphrases. E is the near-miss: the skeptics predicted activist capture, but the passage gives no figure for activists’ share of the vote. A and B are never stated, and C is contradicted (every dollar for water and sewer stays with the council).

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Detail: what does the passage say about the first eight cycles?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, third sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Find “first eight cycles”: low-income neighborhoods’ share of votes > their share of population. Prephrase that, and beware answers that sound like they follow from it.

choices.note: The passage never says the meetings were moved. The fix was in how ballots were collected.
Not stated. The passage reports a neighborhood breakdown, not voters’ history at hearings.
Contradicted. “Every dollar for water and sewer systems” stays with the council.
CORRECT. “Poorest neighborhoods” = lowest-income neighborhoods; “overrepresented among those who voted” = their share of votes exceeded their share of population.
Tempting, because it answers the skeptics’ prediction. But the passage gives no figure for the activists’ share of votes; it reports only the low-income neighborhoods’ share.

questions.stem: The author’s response to the second objection, as it applies to the city discussed in the second paragraph, rests chiefly on
choices: evidence that residents’ choices addressed problems that the city’s engineers had missed
a limit on what residents are permitted to decide, rather than on how they have chosen
evidence that residents chose to replace aging water mains in preference to building new playgrounds
the high proportion of votes cast by residents of the city’s lowest-income neighborhoods
the council’s willingness to fund, from its own share of the budget, projects that residents had rejected
questions.explanation: The second objection is that residents favor visible projects and starve basic infrastructure. The author answers: “Nor has the program crowded out ordinary obligations,” because residents decide only the 2 percent set-aside and the council keeps every dollar for water and sewer. The answer concedes nothing about residents’ preferences; it relies on what residents are not allowed to decide. That is B. A is the dominant trap: it is the next sentence of the paragraph and sounds like a defense of residents’ judgment, but it is offered as a further point, not as the answer to the bias objection. D answers the first objection, and C and E are never stated.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Inference about the argument: how does the author answer “residents favor the visible and starve infrastructure”?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First paragraph, the second objection; second paragraph, the “Nor has the program crowded out…” sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Does the author show that residents in this city actually prefer water mains? No. The author never disputes their tastes. The answer is structural: residents only get to spend 2 percent, and every water and sewer dollar stays with the council, so whatever they prefer, the pipes don’t starve. Most students pick (A), because the crossing sentence comes right after and sounds like “residents choose wisely.” But it starts with “And,” adding a separate point, and one good choice doesn’t show residents avoid flashy projects. The lesson: find the sentence that actually answers the objection, not the one that sounds most pro-resident.

choices.note: Tempting. This is the trap. It is a separate point (“And residents’ choices have often addressed…”), and one well-chosen crossing says nothing about whether residents tend to favor visible projects or whether infrastructure is starved.
CORRECT. The answer to the second objection is that residents control only the set-aside, and the council keeps all water and sewer spending. It leaves residents’ preferences untouched.
Not stated. The passage never says residents chose water mains; the council funds them.
That is the evidence on the first objection (who participates), not the second.
Not stated. The passage never says the council funds projects that residents rejected.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if added to the city’s arrangements, would most directly address the difficulty that the author says remains unresolved (second sentence of the third paragraph)?
choices: Proposal meetings are held on weekend afternoons, and free child care is provided to residents who attend them.
Before each vote, a specific department head is assigned to each proposal and is evaluated partly on how the project fares.
Vote totals for every project are published by neighborhood after each cycle, so that residents can see which areas supported which projects.
Residents receive detailed cost estimates for each proposal before voting, so that fewer poorly chosen projects are approved.
Projects that fail within five years of completion are listed in an annual report on the program that is distributed to every household.
questions.explanation: The unresolved difficulty is the third objection: when a project fails, no one can be held responsible, since council members can blame residents and residents chose as a crowd. B makes a specific official answerable for each project. C and E are the near-misses: they make choices or failures more visible, but a neighborhood is still a crowd and a report blames no one. D might reduce failures but leaves the question of who answers for them untouched, and A addresses the first objection.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Application: which change would fix the accountability problem?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, second sentence; first paragraph, the third objection.

breakdown.analysis: What exactly is unresolved? Not that projects fail, but that when one does, no one is on the hook. Council blames residents; residents are a crowd. So we need a change that puts a particular person on the hook. Several answers sound like “accountability” because they add transparency. Ask of each: after a failure, who now has to answer?

choices.note: Addresses the first objection (who attends meetings), which the author says can be designed away; it does nothing for accountability.
CORRECT. A named official now owns each project’s outcome, so a failure has someone who answers for it.
Tempting: it adds transparency. But a neighborhood’s vote is still a crowd’s vote, so no one in particular answers for a failure.
Fewer failures is not the same as someone answering for the failures that still happen. It treats the symptom, not the gap.
Tempting: it publicizes failures. But listing a failure doesn’t make anyone responsible for it.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most call into question the author’s suggestion that the first objection described in the first paragraph concerns a feature that can be designed away?
choices: Fewer than one resident in ten has cast a ballot in any of the program’s cycles since it began in 2014.
In cities that accept ballots only at public meetings, low-income residents cast a smaller share of the votes than in the city discussed.
Several of the projects chosen by the city’s voters have proved more costly to maintain than the city’s engineers had projected.
The meetings that set the city’s ballot are still held on weeknights and drawn mostly from its wealthier neighborhoods.
Most residents who voted in the program’s early cycles had never before attended a public hearing on the city’s budget.
questions.explanation: The first objection is about the meetings “at which residents decide which proposals will reach the ballot” (first paragraph), but the city’s evidence concerns only who voted (second paragraph). If even this city’s ballot-setting meetings are weeknight affairs dominated by wealthier residents, its design never avoided the problem the critics described, which is D. A is the dominant trap: low turnout sounds unrepresentative, but the author’s evidence is relative (low-income neighborhoods’ share of votes versus their share of population), and a small electorate can still have that composition. B and E support the author, and C concerns cost.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Weaken: find the fact that most undermines the claim that the city designed away the first objection.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First paragraph, the first objection (it is about the proposal meetings); second paragraph (the city’s evidence is about ballots); third paragraph, first sentence.

breakdown.analysis: What exactly did the critics complain about? Not the vote: the weeknight meetings that decide what gets on the ballot. And what did the city fix? The vote: mail ballots, libraries, grocery stores. So did the city avoid the problem the critics described? Only if its meetings were fair too, and the passage never says. We need an answer showing the meetings still skew. That answer looks as if it just repeats the critics, which is why it hides. Most students pick (A), because low turnout feels like a failure of representation. But the author’s evidence is a share, not a count. Watch for count-versus-share swaps.

choices.note: Tempting. This is the trap. Low turnout sounds damning, but the author’s claim rests on who the voters are (share of votes versus share of population), not how many there are. A small electorate can still be a fair sample.
This shows the city’s ballot access works better than the alternative, which supports the author.
Maintenance costs bear at most on which projects get chosen, not on who participates.

CORRECT. The objection targets the ballot-setting meetings. If those are still weeknight affairs dominated by wealthier residents, the city never avoided the problem; it only widened access to the final vote.
New voters who never attend hearings suggest the activists didn’t capture the vote. That supports the author.

questions.stem: The passage is primarily concerned with
choices: arguing that a court decision has in effect ended the public’s right to use the dry-sand beach along a retreating coast
showing that the distinction between erosion and avulsion cannot be applied to beaches and that the easement should therefore roll with every shift
explaining why the Texas Supreme Court preferred a fixed easement to a rolling one in Severance v. Patterson after Hurricane Rita
examining a legal problem posed by a retreating shore, faulting one court’s answer, and urging an alternative chiefly because courts could apply it more reliably
describing how one court resolved a dispute over a retreating shore and recommending, despite its admitted arbitrariness, a test that the court itself considered and rejected
questions.explanation: The passage poses the question of whether the beach easement moves, sets out the court’s middle course, explains why its erosion–avulsion distinction is hard to apply to beaches, and closes by urging Corwin’s test because it asks courts a question the evidence can answer. D captures all three moves. E is the near-miss: it is hedged in the same careful way and does reflect the author’s recommendation, but nothing says the court considered and rejected such a test, and E omits the critique of the court. A turns a warning into a result, B goes beyond the scientists’ doubts, and C misdescribes the court’s middle course.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Primary purpose: what does the passage as a whole do?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Whole passage: the question (first paragraph), the court’s answer (second), its weakness (third), Corwin’s alternative (fourth).

breakdown.analysis: Map it: question → the two obvious answers → the court’s compromise → why the compromise is hard to apply → Corwin’s test, which the author says should win because courts can actually determine where a line has stood. So the right answer has three parts: the problem, a criticism of the court, and a recommendation with its reason. Two answers carry careful qualifications; check each clause against the passage, not the tone.

choices.note: Too strong. The worry that the exception will “become the rule” is a threat the advocates warn of, not a result the author reports.
Goes beyond the passage. The author says the distinction fits beaches poorly and endorses no fully rolling easement.
Misdescribes the decision: the court took a middle course, with an easement that rolls with gradual change but not with sudden change.

CORRECT. The problem (first paragraph), a criticism of the court’s rule (third), and the closing recommendation of a persistence test for its evidentiary merit (“courts could apply it more reliably”).

Tempting, because the author does recommend the test despite conceding its arbitrariness. But the passage never says the court considered Corwin’s test, let alone rejected it, and E leaves out the author’s critique of the court.

questions.stem: The author mentions a neighbor who lost the same thirty meters over twenty years (last sentence of the second paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: suggest that gradual erosion is more common on the Texas coast than sudden loss of land in storms
indicate that the author regards the court’s rule as unfair to owners who lose their land gradually
make concrete a consequence of the court’s rule that turns on something other than the amount of land actually lost
show that the court misunderstood how the older law of boundaries along water treats sudden changes
present a case that the test Corwin proposes would decide differently from the way the court’s rule decides it
questions.explanation: The sentence contrasts two owners who lose the same thirty meters, one in a hurricane and one over twenty years, and reaches opposite results. It makes concrete that, under Severance, the outcome turns on speed rather than on the amount lost, which is C. B gives the author a judgment of unfairness the passage never expresses. E is wrong on the facts: the neighbor’s gradual loss would move the easement under both tests. A and D are not supported.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Function: why the two neighbors?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, last sentence (“Thus…”).

breakdown.analysis: Same loss, thirty meters each, but opposite outcomes. What differs? Only how fast it happened. “Thus” tells you the sentence illustrates the rule just stated. Prephrase: “to show concretely that the rule turns on speed, not on how much land is lost.”

choices.note: The example is about two hypothetical owners, not about how common each kind of loss is.
Tempting, since the results look lopsided. But the author never calls the rule unfair to anyone. Don’t give the author an opinion the passage doesn’t express.
CORRECT. Equal losses, different results: the consequence turns on speed, “something other than the amount of land lost.”
The author never says the court misread the older law; the scientists question whether it fits beaches.
Wrong on the facts. The neighbor’s gradual twenty-year loss moves the easement under Severance and, once the line has stood five years, under Corwin’s test too.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the court in Severance v. Patterson
choices: borrowed from an established body of law a distinction between kinds of change in a shoreline
held that the public’s easement does not move when the vegetation line shifts, however the shift occurs
required the state to compensate owners whose sand became subject to the public’s easement
rejected the view that the Open Beaches Act can give the public a right to sand within privately titled lots
relied on evidence that much apparently gradual retreat of a beach is the cumulative work of many small storms
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says the court took its middle course “drawn from the older law of boundaries along water” and distinguished erosion from avulsion, which A paraphrases. B is the near-miss: the easement stays put only for sudden change and follows gradual change. E gives the court the coastal scientists’ point, which the third paragraph uses against the court’s rule. C has no basis (compensation is never discussed), and D contradicts the first paragraph.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Detail: what does the passage say the court did?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: The court took a distinction from “the older law of boundaries along water”: gradual erosion versus sudden avulsion. The right answer says that in other words (“established body of law”, “kinds of change”). The wrong answers borrow real content from the wrong paragraph or drop half the rule.

choices.note: CORRECT. “Older law of boundaries along water” = an established body of law; erosion versus avulsion = kinds of change in a shoreline.
Half right. That is the rule for sudden change only; gradual change carries the easement with it.
Not in the passage. Compensation is never discussed; the court only required the state to establish the public’s right anew after sudden change.
Contradicts the first paragraph: the Act lets the public use such sand where it has acquired a right to it.
Wrong party. That is the coastal scientists’ point, raised against the court’s distinction.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information in the passage?
choices: Under the rule announced in Severance v. Patterson, an owner whose vegetation line retreated gradually could exclude the public from the sand exposed, if the retreat continued for many years.
Under Corwin’s test, the public’s easement would move to a new vegetation line as soon as the line had shifted, provided that the shift had occurred gradually.
Corwin’s test would let some owners keep the public, for a time, off sand exposed by gradual erosion that the court’s rule would open at once.
Under Corwin’s test, the public could begin using sand exposed by a hurricane sooner than it could under the rule announced in Severance v. Patterson.
The coastal scientists who doubt the court’s distinction would regard Corwin’s test as fairer to coastal landowners than the rule announced in Severance v. Patterson.
questions.explanation: Under the court’s rule the easement follows gradual change, so creeping erosion opens the newly exposed sand at once (second paragraph). Under Corwin’s test the easement moves only after a shift has persisted five years (fourth paragraph), so an owner losing sand gradually keeps the public off it until then. That is C, which combines the two paragraphs. D is the dominant trap: Corwin’s test eventually opens storm-exposed sand, but under the court’s rule the state may establish the public’s right anew, possibly sooner, so the passage does not show Corwin’s test is faster. A and B reverse the two rules, and E attributes a view to the scientists that they never express.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Inference: which comparison of the two approaches does the passage support?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph (the court’s rule, including “establish the public’s right to that sand anew”) and fourth paragraph (Corwin’s five-year test).

breakdown.analysis: Most readers think of Corwin’s test as the pro-public fix for hurricanes, and it is, eventually. But look at the other kind of loss. The court’s rule moves the easement with gradual erosion as it happens. Corwin’s test moves nothing until a shift has lasted five years, “however the shift occurred.” So for gradual erosion her test is slower: an owner keeps the sand private for a while. The right answer describes that without saying “gradual” (“some owners”, “sand the court’s rule would open as soon as it was exposed”). Most students pick (D). It sounds right, but under the court’s rule the state can establish the public’s right anew, and nothing says that takes longer than five years.

choices.note: Reverses the court’s rule. Gradual retreat carries the public’s right with it, however long it continues.
Contradicts Corwin’s test, which waits five years whatever the cause, gradual shifts included.

CORRECT. Gradual erosion opens the sand at once under the court’s rule (“a beach that creeps inland carries the public’s right with it”); under Corwin’s test the owner keeps it private until the shift has lasted five years.

Tempting. This is the trap. Corwin’s test opens storm-exposed sand after five years, but under the court’s rule the state may establish the public’s right anew, and the passage gives no reason to think that takes longer. “Sooner” isn’t supported.
The scientists only doubt that the distinction can be applied; the passage says nothing about how they would view Corwin’s test or fairness to owners.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, in which one of the following disputes would a court applying the rule announced in Severance v. Patterson and a court applying the test Corwin proposes reach different conclusions about whether the public may use the sand in question?
choices: Two years ago a storm stripped away an owner’s dunes, but sand has since rebuilt them and the vegetation line is back where it was; the owner wants to fence the beach seaward of that line.
Over thirty years, gradual erosion carried a vegetation line forty meters inland, where it has stood for the past decade; the owner wants to fence the sand seaward of the new line.
Ten years ago a hurricane moved an owner’s vegetation line fifteen meters inland, where it has stayed, and the state has made no new showing of a public right to the exposed sand.
Three months ago a hurricane moved an owner’s vegetation line ten meters inland; the owner wants to fence the sand that the storm exposed.
Eight years ago a hurricane moved an owner’s vegetation line twenty meters inland, where it has stayed, and the state has since proved a public right to the exposed sand.
questions.explanation: Under the court’s rule, a sudden shift leaves storm-exposed sand free of the easement unless the state establishes the public’s right anew; under Corwin’s test, any shift that persists five years moves the easement. In C the shift was sudden, has lasted ten years, and the state has made no new showing, so the court’s rule lets the owner fence while Corwin’s test opens the sand. D is the main trap: three months is too short for Corwin’s test to move the easement, so both let the owner fence. E is the other near-miss: the state’s proof opens the sand under the court’s rule too. In A and B both approaches agree.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Application: in which dispute do the two approaches give different answers?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph (the court’s rule and “establish … anew”) and fourth paragraph (the five-year test).

breakdown.analysis: Build a two-column table. Court: gradual moves the easement; sudden doesn’t, unless the state proves a new right. Corwin: lasted five years? Moves. Otherwise nothing changes. Now run each case. You need sudden + over five years + no new proof. The traps are a hurricane case that is too recent for Corwin’s test to bite (D) and one where the state’s proof makes the court’s rule open the sand anyway (E).

choices.note: Both agree. The line is back where it was, so the sand seaward of it is still subject to the easement under either approach.
Both agree. Gradual change moves the easement under the court’s rule, and the line has stood at its new place for over five years, so it moves under Corwin’s test too.
CORRECT. Sudden shift and no new showing: the owner may fence under the court’s rule. Lasted ten years: the easement moves under Corwin’s test.
Tempting. This is the trap. Hurricane cases are where the two differ, but only after five years. At three months Corwin’s test changes nothing, so both let the owner fence.
Tempting, since it is a lasting hurricane shift. But the state has proved a public right, which opens the sand under the court’s rule as well.

questions.stem: Which one of the following statements about the test Corwin proposes is most strongly supported by the passage?
choices: It would answer the objection that a rolling easement shifts public use onto land that its owners never surrendered to the public.
It would apply only to shifts caused by storms, leaving gradual change to be handled as the court’s rule handles it.
It would prevent owners from excluding the public from any of the sand that a storm has exposed.
It was devised chiefly to keep the exception for sudden change from coming, as public access advocates feared, to govern most of the Texas coast.
It would tie the public’s right to a matter the evidence can settle more readily than the one on which the court’s rule turns.
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph says the test’s “chief merit is evidentiary”: courts would determine where a line has stood rather than reconstruct how quickly it got there, and the third paragraph says the physical record often cannot answer the speed question. E puts the two together. D is the main trap: the test might ease the advocates’ worry, but the passage names its chief merit as evidentiary and says nothing about why Corwin devised it. A fails because the test still moves the easement onto private land, B contradicts “however the shift occurred,” and C ignores the five-year wait.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Inference: what does the passage support about Corwin’s test?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph (“chief merit is evidentiary”) with the third paragraph (the physical record and the speed question).

breakdown.analysis: What does Corwin’s test change? The question a court asks: not how fast the line moved, but where it has stood. Why is that better? The third paragraph says the record often can’t tell how fast a line moved. So her test swaps a hard-to-prove fact for an easier one. The right answer says that abstractly. The trap names a purpose (the advocates’ worry) the passage never assigns to the test.

choices.note: Her test still moves the easement onto land once a shift has lasted five years, so owners’ objection to a rolling easement stands.
Contradicts the passage: the easement moves “however the shift occurred.”
Too strong. For the first five years after a storm, nothing changes, so owners can still exclude the public.
Tempting, because the advocates’ warning is just before Corwin’s paragraph. But the passage gives her test’s chief merit as evidentiary and says nothing about why she devised it.
CORRECT. “A matter the evidence can settle more readily” = where a line has stood; “the one on which the court’s rule turns” = how quickly it moved, which the physical record often cannot show.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Measurements at a subarctic colony show that dark eggs take nearly twice as long as pale eggs to cool to the temperature at which embryos stop developing.
The finding that eggs are darker in colder regions shows that concealment plays little part in determining the color of birds’ eggs.
The tendency of eggs to be darker where it is cold may, for some ground-nesting birds, reflect a developmental benefit that outweighs a cost in concealment.
Ground-nesting shorebirds whose eggs are darker than the surrounding ground lose more clutches to predators than those whose eggs match it.
Because dark eggs are more easily found by predators, the darkening of eggs in colder regions remains unexplained by any current hypothesis.
questions.explanation: The passage presents a puzzle (darker eggs in cold regions, despite the value of camouflage), a warmth explanation that the survey’s authors proposed and Varga develops for some shorebirds (darkness slows cooling and so shortens incubation), evidence for it, and a test that could confirm it. C captures the explanation with the passage’s own hedge (“for some ground-nesting shorebirds”). A is the near-miss: it accurately reports the third paragraph’s numbers but is evidence, not the point. B overstates (predators do find dark clutches more often), D contradicts the hatching data, and E ignores Varga’s account.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Main point: what is the passage mainly arguing?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First paragraph (the puzzle and the survey authors’ warmth proposal), second (Varga’s version of it), third and fourth (evidence and a proposed test).

breakdown.analysis: Phenomenon → hypothesis → evidence. The hypothesis is the point: for some shorebirds, dark eggs pay because they slow cooling, which shortens incubation, and that gain beats the lost camouflage. Prephrase: “Darker eggs in cold places may be a warmth adaptation whose benefit outweighs its camouflage cost.” The hardest wrong answer is a true number from the evidence paragraph.

choices.note: Tempting, because it is accurate (about 28 minutes versus 15). But it’s one measurement offered as support, not the passage’s point.
Too strong. Camouflage still matters: darker clutches were found by predators more often. Varga’s claim is that the warmth gain outweighs it.
CORRECT. “Developmental benefit” = fewer pauses in development; “outweighs a cost in concealment” = Varga’s trade-off; “may” and “for some” match the passage’s hedges.
Contradicted where it matters: in the northern colonies, darker clutches hatched more often overall.
Ignores the whole second paragraph. The passage offers Varga’s account as a plausible explanation.

questions.stem: According to the passage, at the colony near the southern edge of the species’ range
choices: dark eggs are found by predators less often than pale eggs are
even pale eggs cool far more slowly than pale eggs at the subarctic colony do
eggs are paler, on average, than those laid at the subarctic colony
dark eggs take about 28 minutes to cool to the developmental threshold
females’ foraging trips are shorter than those of females at the subarctic colony
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says that at the southern colony even pale eggs took more than an hour to cool to the threshold, compared with about 15 minutes at the subarctic colony. B states that comparison. E is the near-miss: the passage says the trips there were “no longer than” in the north, which does not say they were shorter. C is what the survey’s pattern might lead one to expect, but the passage never reports egg color there, and D is the subarctic colony’s figure for dark eggs.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Detail: what does the passage say about the southern colony?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, last sentence, against the subarctic figures earlier in that paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: The passage gives two facts about the southern colony: trips “no longer than in the north,” and warmer air, so even pale eggs took “more than an hour” to cool. Compare: a pale egg in the north took about 15 minutes. That’s the answer. Watch “no longer than”: it means equal or shorter, not shorter.

choices.note: Not stated. Predation is discussed only for the northern colonies.
CORRECT. More than an hour versus about 15 minutes for a pale egg in the north.
Plausible given the survey’s cold-to-dark pattern, but the passage never reports the color of eggs at the southern colony.
Wrong colony. About 28 minutes is the figure for dark eggs at the subarctic colony.
Tempting. This is the trap. “No longer than in the north” allows trips of the same length; it doesn’t say they were shorter.

questions.stem: By “day for day” (third sentence of the fourth paragraph), the author most probably means
choices: as a rate per day, apart from how long each clutch is exposed
on every single day of the incubation period, without any exception
over the whole period from the laying of the eggs to their hatching
during the daylight hours in which females leave the nest to forage
in proportion to the number of eggs that each clutch contains
questions.explanation: The sentence contrasts a total (darker clutches hatched more often “overall”) with a rate (predators found them more often “day for day”). The phrase means per day of exposure, apart from how many days a clutch is exposed, which is A; that is how darker clutches can be found more often per day yet survive more often, since they spend fewer days in the nest. C is the opposite (the overall figure), B takes the phrase literally, and D and E substitute other measures.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Meaning in context: what does “day for day” mean here?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph, third sentence; second paragraph on extra days in the nest.

breakdown.analysis: How can darker clutches be found by predators more often and still hatch more often? Only if “more often” is a rate per day, while darker clutches spend fewer days in the nest. “Overall” is the total; “day for day” is the daily rate. Rate versus total is a classic LSAT distinction; know it.

choices.note: CORRECT. A per-day rate that sets aside how many days each clutch is exposed; that’s what lets the overall hatching figure come out the other way.
Too literal and too strong. The phrase doesn’t claim dark clutches were found more often on every single day.
Opposite. The whole-period figure is the “overall” one, on which darker clutches do better.
Reads “day” as daylight. The phrase isn’t about time of day.
Clutch size is never discussed.

questions.stem: The author mentions the island colony and the valley colony (second sentence of the fourth paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: show that egg color follows the factor Varga stresses rather than another one that usually accompanies it
suggest that predators of ground nests are less numerous on exposed islands than in sheltered valleys
supply the temperature figures used in the calculations described in the third paragraph
anticipate the result that the clutch exchange proposed in the last sentences of the paragraph is meant to confirm
show that the 2020 survey’s finding about latitude does not hold within a single species
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says wind hastens an egg’s cooling much as cold air does, so eggs at the exposed, wind-scoured island cool faster than eggs in the sheltered valley, though both lie at the same latitude. Since latitude and rapid cooling usually go together, the pair separates them, and darkness follows the cooling, the factor in Varga’s account. That is A. E is the near-miss: the survey linked darkness to colder regions, not to latitude as such, and the pair is consistent with it. D misreads the proposed exchange, which tests shell against female traits, and B and C are unsupported.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Function: why compare an island colony with a valley colony at the same latitude?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph, second sentence; second paragraph (wind hastens cooling “much as cold air does”).

breakdown.analysis: Why insist on “the same latitude”? Because north usually means cold and fast-cooling eggs, so a north–south pattern alone can’t tell you which one drives darkness. Now connect the second paragraph: wind cools eggs much as cold air does, so the wind-scoured island is the fast-cooling site. Hold latitude fixed, vary the cooling, and darkness follows the cooling. Prephrase: “to pull cooling apart from latitude and show color tracks cooling.” The right answer says this abstractly, without naming either factor, which is what makes it hard.

choices.note: CORRECT. The factor Varga stresses is how fast eggs cool; wind does that work at the island (second paragraph). The factor that “usually accompanies it” is latitude. The pair holds latitude fixed, and darkness follows the cooling.
Predator numbers aren’t compared, and the example concerns egg color.
The third paragraph’s figures come from the subarctic and southern colonies, not these two.
The exchange tests whether the shell or some trait of the females drives hatching success. The island comparison is offered as existing evidence, not as a forecast of that test’s result.
Tempting, since latitude is the hook. But the survey tied darkness to colder regions, not to latitude as such, and the island colony fits that finding.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements about the view that egg color serves for concealment (first paragraph)?
choices: It has been shown by the observations at the northern colonies to be mistaken about how egg color affects the risk of predation.
It identifies a real disadvantage of dark eggs, one that Varga’s account treats as outweighed rather than as illusory.
It adequately explains the color of birds’ eggs everywhere except in regions where the breeding-season air is cold.
It wrongly takes for granted that predators of ground nests locate eggs chiefly by sight.
It accounts for the difference in egg color between the island colony and the valley colony.
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph reports that predators found darker clutches “somewhat more often day for day,” so the concealment cost is real, and Varga contends that the warmth gain “outweighs the loss of camouflage” (second paragraph). The account keeps the cost and weighs it, which is B. A reverses the evidence, which confirms the concealment effect. E is the near-miss: the island comparison does concern egg color, but the author offers it as support for the warmth account, and nothing is said about the ground at either colony. C overstates the passage’s scope, and D is never suggested.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Author agrees: what does the author think of the camouflage view?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First paragraph (the view), second paragraph (“outweighs the loss of camouflage”), fourth paragraph (the predation data and the island comparison).

breakdown.analysis: Does Varga’s account say camouflage doesn’t matter? No. Her claim is a trade-off: dark eggs lose camouflage, and the warmth gain is bigger. And the data back the cost: darker clutches were found more often day for day. So the camouflage view is right about the cost and wrong only in thinking the cost settles the matter. The hard part: the right answer talks about the old view in terms of the new one.

choices.note: Backward. The northern observations confirm that darker clutches are found more often, just as the concealment view predicts.
CORRECT. The cost (more predation per day) is real; Varga’s account says the warmth gain outweighs it, not that it isn’t there.
Too broad. The passage discusses ground-nesting shorebirds and never says the concealment view adequately explains egg color everywhere else.
Never suggested. How predators find eggs isn’t discussed.

Tempting, because the island and valley eggs differ in color. But the author cites that difference as evidence for the warmth account (“point the same way”), and the passage says nothing about the color of the ground at either site.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most call into question Varga’s account as described in the second paragraph?
choices: Among northern colonies with similar air temperatures during incubation, clutches are no darker where skies are usually clear than where they are usually overcast.
At northern colonies, predators find darker clutches more often, day for day, than they find paler clutches at the same sites.
In shorebird species in which both parents take turns incubating, so that eggs are seldom left uncovered, eggs are no darker in cold regions than in warm ones.
Producing the pigment that darkens the shells requires energy that the female must replace by foraging.
Few of the species included in the 2020 survey of eggshell color were ground-nesting shorebirds in which only one parent incubates.
questions.explanation: Varga’s mechanism is that dark shells “absorb more sunlight” and so cool more slowly. With temperature held constant, the benefit should be greatest where skies are clear; if eggs are no darker there than under cloud, the trait does not track the benefit said to explain it. That is A. B is the dominant trap: it attacks a cost the account already concedes, since the fourth paragraph reports exactly this predation pattern and Varga argues the gain outweighs it. C supports the account (with eggs rarely uncovered, there is no cooling problem to solve), D adds a small cost without touching the trade-off, and E concerns the survey, not the shorebird evidence.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Weaken: what most damages the claim that dark eggs are an adaptation for warmth?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph (the mechanism: absorbing sunlight); fourth paragraph (the predation pattern the account already accepts).

breakdown.analysis: Where does the warmth come from in Varga’s story? Sunlight. So with the air equally cold, where should darkness pay most? Under clear skies.
