If darkness ignores the sky, it doesn’t follow its supposed payoff. The right answer looks like a weather fact, which is why it hides. Most students pick (B), because “dark eggs get eaten more” sounds like the obvious objection. But the passage already grants it; the account is a trade-off. Attacking a cost the argument concedes doesn’t weaken it.

choices.note: CORRECT. Temperature held equal, the sunlight benefit is largest under clear skies. Finding no extra darkness there cuts the trait loose from its proposed benefit.
Tempting. This is the trap. The passage already reports this, and Varga’s account says the warmth gain outweighs it. A trade-off isn’t hurt by its admitted cost.
Fits the account. If eggs are rarely left uncovered, there is no cooling problem for darkness to solve, so no cline is expected.
One more cost doesn’t show the warmth benefit is missing or too small; Varga already argues the benefit outweighs costs.
Irrelevant to Varga’s account, which rests on the cooling mechanism and the shorebird figures, not on the survey’s species mix.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information in the passage?
choices: Over a full incubation at the subarctic colony, the embryo in a dark egg would never have its development halted.
At the subarctic colony, a dark shell would spare an embryo more developmental delay on a 40-minute foraging trip than on a 25-minute one.
At the subarctic colony, pale eggs take about twice as long as dark eggs do to cool to the developmental threshold in sunlight.
If trips at the subarctic colony averaged about 20 minutes, dark eggs there would offer no developmental advantage over pale eggs.
At the colony near the southern edge of the range, dark eggs would take more than two hours to cool to the developmental threshold.
questions.explanation: At the subarctic colony a pale egg reaches the 26°C threshold in about 15 minutes and a dark egg in about 28. On a 25-minute trip the pale egg’s embryo pauses about 10 minutes and the dark egg’s not at all, a saving of about 10. On a 40-minute trip the pale egg pauses about 25 minutes and the dark egg about 12, a saving of about 13. So the dark shell spares more on the longer trip, which is B. D is the dominant trap: on a 20-minute trip the pale egg still pauses about 5 minutes and the dark egg not at all. A turns “typical” trips into all trips, C reverses the cooling times, and E goes beyond the figures given.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Inference with numbers: what follows from the cooling times?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph: pale egg about 15 minutes to the threshold, dark egg about 28, trips about 25.

breakdown.analysis: Write the numbers down: pale hits 26°C at about 15 min; dark at about 28. Pause = trip length minus time to threshold (if positive). 25-min trip: pale 10, dark 0 → saving 10. 40-min trip: pale 25, dark 12 → saving 13. Intuition says the dark shell’s edge fades once it too crosses the threshold, but the saving is capped at 28 − 15 = 13 minutes, and a 25-minute trip doesn’t reach that cap. Most students reject (B) on feel and pick (D), because 20 minutes sounds “short enough.” But the pale egg still crosses at 15. Do the subtraction; don’t go by feel.

choices.note: Too strong. The 28-minute figure beats the typical 25-minute trip, but trip lengths are averages; any trip over about 28 minutes would halt development.
CORRECT. 25-minute trip: pale pauses ≈10, dark 0, saving ≈10. 40-minute trip: pale ≈25, dark ≈12, saving ≈13. The saving keeps growing until the trip reaches about 28 minutes, then holds at about 13.
Reversed. Dark eggs take about twice as long (28 minutes versus 15).
Tempting. This is the trap. On a 20-minute trip the pale egg is below the threshold for about 5 minutes and the dark egg not at all, so dark eggs still help.
No figure supports “more than two hours”; the passage says only that pale eggs there take more than an hour.

questions.stimulus: Personal-finance columnist Nora Pruitt advises her readers to keep enough savings on hand to cover six months of living expenses. Yet in a recent interview, Pruitt admitted that she herself has rarely kept more than two months' worth of expenses in savings. Clearly, then, her advice about saving is not worth following.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: fails to consider that many of the columnist's readers may already keep six months of expenses in savings
presumes, without providing justification, that the columnist described her own savings habits accurately in the interview
draws a conclusion about all of the columnist's financial advice from evidence about her advice on a single topic
takes for granted that advice cannot be sound if the person who gives it does not follow it
relies on the opinion of a newspaper columnist rather than on the judgment of trained financial experts
questions.explanation: The argument rejects Pruitt's advice because Pruitt doesn't follow it herself, but whether advice is sound has nothing to do with whether the adviser takes it; (D) names this. (C) is the tempting misreading: the conclusion is only about her advice on saving, not all her advice. (B) objects to a premise rather than the reasoning, and (A) and (E) describe reasoning the argument never uses.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Pruitt's advice about saving is not worth following.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Pruitt advises six months of savings; Pruitt herself rarely keeps more than two months of savings.

breakdown.analysis: So what if Pruitt doesn't follow her own advice? A smoker who tells you smoking is bad for you is still right. Whether advice is good depends on the reasons for it, not on the adviser's habits. This is a classic: rejecting a claim because the person making it doesn't practice it (tu quoque, a kind of ad hominem). Know it. We need an answer that says the argument treats the adviser's behavior as proof the advice is bad.

choices.note: Wrong. What readers already do has nothing to do with whether the advice is sound. The argument never relies on how many readers follow it.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Most drivers already wear seat belts, so a campaign urging seat-belt use will change nothing.

choices.note: Wrong. This objects to a premise, not the reasoning. The flaw remains even if the interview was perfectly accurate: her habits still wouldn't show the advice is bad.
Tempting, because the argument does generalize. But look at the conclusion: it's only about 'her advice about saving,' which is the topic the evidence concerns. No jump from one topic to all of them.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Her advice on mortgages was poor, so none of her financial advice can be trusted.

choices.note: CORRECT. That's exactly the leap: Pruitt doesn't take her advice, so the advice must be bad. A person's failure to follow advice says nothing about whether the advice is good.
Wrong. The argument doesn't rely on Pruitt's opinion at all; it rejects her advice. This describes an appeal to authority the argument never makes.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: A famous actor says this diet works, so it must work.

questions.stimulus: Theater critic: The Harrow Playhouse's productions of new plays by local writers sell fewer tickets than its revivals of familiar classics, and some board members now want to drop the new plays. That would be a mistake. Several plays that premiered at the Harrow have gone on to successful runs elsewhere, and that reputation for discovery is a major reason donors continue to support the playhouse.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion drawn in the argument?
choices: The Harrow's productions of new plays by local writers sell fewer tickets than its revivals of familiar classics.
Donors support the Harrow Playhouse mainly because of its reputation for discovering promising new plays.
The Harrow Playhouse should stage more new plays by local writers and fewer revivals of familiar classics.
The Harrow's reputation for discovery is worth more to the playhouse than the ticket sales the new plays lose.
The Harrow Playhouse would be making a mistake if it stopped staging new plays by local writers.
questions.explanation: The conclusion is the short middle sentence, 'That would be a mistake,' which refers back to dropping the new plays; (E) spells it out. (A) is background, (B) overstates a premise ('a major reason' is not 'mainly'), (C) goes further than the critic, and (D) is an unstated bridge the critic might accept but never asserts.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Dropping the new plays by local writers would be a mistake.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Several Harrow premieres went on to successful runs elsewhere; that reputation for discovery is a major reason donors keep supporting the playhouse.

breakdown.analysis: The first sentence is background: a fact about ticket sales and a proposal from the board. The conclusion hides in four words: 'That would be a mistake.' What would? Dropping the new plays. Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. Why would it be a mistake? Because of the premieres' success and the donors. Prephrase: the playhouse shouldn't drop its new local plays.

choices.note: Wrong. That's background the critic concedes. It's the reason some board members want the change, not the critic's point.
Wrong. Distorts a premise. The critic says the reputation is 'a major reason' donors give, not the main one. And even accurately stated, it's support, not the conclusion.
Wrong. Goes too far. The critic argues against dropping the new plays, not for staging more of them.

Tempting, because the critic's reasoning seems to lean on something like this. But the critic never says it, and an unstated bridge isn't the conclusion. The conclusion is about what the playhouse should do.
CORRECT. 'That would be a mistake' refers to dropping the new plays. This says the same thing in different words.

questions.stimulus:
Ruiz: The Brookfield Public Library's main branch should stay open until 10 p.m. on weekdays. Many residents work until 6 p.m. or later, and the current 7 p.m. closing time leaves them almost no chance to use the library during the week.

Okafor: The library's budget is fixed, so longer hours would mean buying fewer new books. Residents who work late can still visit on Saturdays, and most of what the library offers is available online at any hour.
questions.stem: Ruiz and Okafor disagree over whether
choices: many Brookfield residents work until 6 p.m. or later
most of the library's offerings can be used online at any hour
residents who work late are able to visit the library on Saturdays
the library's main branch should stay open until 10 p.m. on weekdays
the library's budget should be increased to pay for keeping the main branch open longer
questions.explanation: Ruiz proposes the later weekday closing, and Okafor gives reasons against adopting it (fewer books, and other ways to use the library), so they disagree about (D). Okafor never disputes that many residents work late (A), and Ruiz says nothing about online offerings (B) or Saturday visits (C); (C) is tempting because Okafor raises it, but Ruiz's complaint is specifically about weekdays. Neither proposes a larger budget (E).

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Ruiz: The main branch should stay open until 10 p.m. on weekdays because many residents work until 6 or later and can't get there before 7; Okafor: Longer hours would cost new books, late workers can come Saturdays, and most offerings are online.

breakdown.analysis: Okafor never says 'no' in so many words, but every point is a reason against the later hours. Ruiz proposes; Okafor rebuts. To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. On the 10 p.m. weekday closing, Ruiz says yes and Okafor clearly says no. Prephrase: whether the library should stay open later on weekdays.

choices.note: Wrong. Ruiz says it, but Okafor never disputes it. In fact Okafor talks about 'residents who work late' as if they exist. No disagreement.
Wrong. Only Okafor talks about online offerings. Ruiz has no stated view, so you can't say they disagree.

Wrong. Tempting because Okafor raises Saturdays as a response. But Ruiz's complaint is specifically about weekdays and never says late workers can't come on Saturday. Ruiz has no stated position here.
CORRECT. Ruiz explicitly says the branch should stay open until 10 p.m. on weekdays. Okafor's whole response is a set of reasons not to do it. Yes versus no.
Wrong. Neither speaker proposes raising the budget. Okafor treats the budget as fixed, and Ruiz never mentions it.

questions.stimulus: In a survey of 400 office workers, those who said they ate breakfast every day reported feeling noticeably more alert during morning meetings than did those who said they usually skipped breakfast. Hence, eating breakfast increases a person's alertness in the morning.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Most of the surveyed workers who usually skipped breakfast also reported getting far less sleep than the breakfast eaters did.
Many of the office workers surveyed said that they drank coffee during their morning meetings.
Office workers who usually skip breakfast tend to eat a noticeably larger lunch than office workers who eat breakfast.
Several of the surveyed workers who ate breakfast every day said that a heavy breakfast sometimes left them feeling sluggish.
Some nutritionists recommend a light breakfast rather than a large one for people who have meetings early in the day.
questions.explanation: The argument moves from a correlation to the claim that breakfast causes alertness. (A) offers an alternative cause: the breakfast skippers also sleep much less, which could explain their lower alertness. (B) would matter only if coffee drinking differed between the groups, which it doesn't say; (D) concerns only a few workers and only sometimes; (C) concerns lunch and (E) concerns advice, not cause.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Eating breakfast increases a person's alertness in the morning.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: In a survey of 400 office workers, daily breakfast eaters reported feeling more alert in morning meetings than breakfast skippers.

breakdown.analysis: Correlation to causation. Breakfast eaters feel more alert, so breakfast causes alertness. But maybe the breakfast eaters differ in some other way that explains it. To weaken, find that other difference. Prephrase: the two groups differ in something like sleep or overall habits. It's like saying people who own running shoes are fitter, so buying running shoes makes you fit.

choices.note: CORRECT. An alternative cause. The skippers sleep far less, and lack of sleep would make anyone less alert. Breakfast may have nothing to do with it.
Tempting, because coffee affects alertness. But nothing says one group drank more coffee than the other. A factor shared by both groups can't explain the difference between them.
Wrong. Lunch comes after the morning meetings. A bigger lunch can't explain how alert people felt before it.

Tempting, because it sounds like breakfast sometimes hurts alertness. But it's only several workers, only sometimes, and only after a heavy breakfast. The group as a whole still reported more alertness.
Irrelevant. What some nutritionists recommend says nothing about whether breakfast causes alertness.

questions.stimulus: Ornithologists studying marsh wrens in the Teller Wetlands found that each male builds several dummy nests in addition to the nest in which eggs are laid. Building these extra nests costs the birds considerable time and energy. Yet wrens that build more dummy nests tend to raise more chicks than wrens that build fewer.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Predators that find an empty dummy nest often abandon their search before finding the nest that holds eggs.
Dummy nests are usually built from the same materials and in the same shape as the nests that hold eggs.
Male wrens that build many dummy nests spend less time than other males gathering food for their chicks.
Some other bird species in the Teller Wetlands also build nests in which they never lay eggs.
Female wrens typically lay the same number of eggs regardless of how many nests the male has built.
questions.explanation: Dummy nests are costly, yet wrens that build more of them raise more chicks. (A) shows a payoff that outweighs the cost: decoy nests send predators away before they reach the eggs. (B) makes the decoys look convincing but never says they do anything; (C) adds a cost and deepens the puzzle; (E) rules out one possible benefit; (D) is about other species.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Dummy nests cost wrens a lot of time and energy, but wrens that build more of them raise more chicks.

breakdown.analysis: How can a costly, useless-looking habit go with more chicks? We need a benefit from the dummy nests that outweighs the cost. Prephrase: the dummy nests protect the real nest somehow, like decoys. Think of a shell game: hide the prize under one of five cups and a thief has worse odds than with one cup.

choices.note: CORRECT. Decoys. Predators waste their search on empty nests and give up before finding the eggs. More dummy nests, more eggs survive, more chicks. Both facts now fit.
Tempting, because it makes the decoys look real. But it never says looking real helps the chicks. It's half a mechanism.
Wrong. This adds another cost of building dummy nests. Less food for the chicks makes the result even more puzzling.
Irrelevant. Other species' habits don't explain why more dummy nests go with more wren chicks.
Wrong. This rules out one possible benefit (more eggs). It leaves the puzzle in place.

questions.stimulus: A panel of professional chefs tasted each of the twelve sauces that the Mirela Bistro has developed for its new menu and rated every one of them excellent. Each dish on the new menu will combine one of these sauces with a main ingredient that the bistro already prepares superbly. So every dish on the new menu will be excellent.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: fails to consider whether diners will pay more for the dishes on the new menu than for the old ones
relies on the ratings of chefs who may have had a hand in developing the sauces they were asked to judge
takes for granted that a dish cannot be excellent unless the sauce in it is excellent
treats the success of the bistro's current dishes as proof that its new menu will be equally popular
takes for granted that combining elements that are each excellent on their own will produce something excellent
questions.explanation: The argument moves from the excellence of each component (every sauce, every main ingredient) to the excellence of every combination, but two excellent components can still make a poor dish; (E) names this part-to-whole assumption. (B) is tempting because biased judges are a familiar flaw, but nothing suggests the chefs helped develop the sauces. (C) reverses the argument's conditional (it treats excellent sauces as sufficient, not necessary), and (A) and (D) raise price and popularity, which the conclusion never mentions.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Every dish on the bistro's new menu will be excellent.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: All twelve new sauces were rated excellent; each dish pairs one of those sauces with a main ingredient the bistro already prepares superbly.

breakdown.analysis: So what if every part is excellent? Great parts don't guarantee a great whole. A superb sauce can clash with a superb piece of fish. It's like arguing: every player on this team is an all-star, so the team will be great. Maybe, but they still have to play well together. This is the part-to-whole flaw (composition). It's a classic; know it. Prephrase: the argument assumes that excellent components automatically make an excellent combination.

choices.note: Wrong. Price is a different dimension. The conclusion is about whether the dishes will be excellent, not whether diners will pay for them.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The new dishes are excellent, so diners will gladly pay twice as much for them.

choices.note: Tempting, because biased judges are a real flaw. But nothing says the chefs had any role in developing the sauces. You can't pick an answer on a possibility the stimulus never raises.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The sauces must be excellent, since the chefs who invented them all rated them highly.

choices.note: Tempting, because it reuses the stimulus's terms. But it reverses the argument's logic. The argument says an excellent sauce (plus an excellent ingredient) is enough for an excellent dish; it never says an excellent sauce is required.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Only dishes with excellent sauces win awards, so this dish, with its excellent sauce, will win one.

choices.note: Wrong. The argument never mentions popularity or the current menu's success. It's about quality, and it relies on the main ingredients being prepared superbly, not on past sales.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Our old menu sold well, so our new menu will sell just as well.

choices.note: CORRECT. The argument goes from 'each sauce is excellent' and 'each ingredient is prepared superbly' to 'each combination is excellent.' That skips whether the pieces work together.

questions.stimulus: Last year the Coralton Water Authority began sending some of its customers monthly reports comparing their water use with that of similar nearby households. Over the following year, customers who received the reports used 4 percent less water than they had the year before. The authority concludes that the reports led those customers to reduce their water use.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the authority's argument?
choices: Water rates in Coralton's service area rose noticeably during the year in which the reports were first being sent out.
Customers randomly chosen not to receive the reports used about as much water as they had the year before.
Many of the customers who received the reports said that they found the comparisons in them confusing or hard to interpret.
Several other water utilities in the region have recently begun sending similar comparison reports to their own customers.
On average, customers who received the reports used more water than the similar households they were compared with.
questions.explanation: The argument attributes a drop in use to the reports, so it is vulnerable to other causes that would have reduced everyone's use. (B) supplies a control group: comparable customers without reports did not cut back, which makes the reports the likely cause. (A) is a trap that actually weakens by offering an alternative cause (higher water rates), and (C), (D), and (E) do not show that the reports caused the drop.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The comparison reports led customers to cut their water use.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Customers who got the reports used 4 percent less water than the year before.

breakdown.analysis: Another causal argument with no comparison. Maybe everyone used less last year, thanks to mild weather, rate hikes, or new water-saving fixtures. To strengthen, rule out those alternatives. Best tool: a control group. If similar customers who didn't get reports didn't cut back, the reports look like the cause. Prephrase: customers without reports didn't reduce their use.

choices.note: Wrong. This is a trap that weakens. Higher water rates are an alternative reason customers would use less water, reports or not.

CORRECT. A random control group. Customers randomly kept from getting reports used about the same as before, so whatever changed last year wasn't pushing everyone down. That points to the reports as the cause of the 4 percent drop.
Wrong. If anything, confusing reports make it less likely they changed behavior. Doesn't strengthen.
Wrong. What other utilities are doing tells you nothing about whether Coralton's reports worked.
Wrong. Knowing they started out above their neighbors might suggest a motive to cut back, but it doesn't show the reports actually caused the drop. Other causes are still on the table.

questions.stimulus: Geologist: A layer of volcanic ash in the cliffs above Maren Bay matches, in chemical composition, the ash produced by an eruption of Mount Askel about 9,000 years ago. Ash from a single eruption usually has a chemical signature that can be distinguished from the ash of other eruptions. Therefore, the sediment layers lying directly beneath this ash in the cliffs were deposited more than about 9,000 years ago.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the geologist's argument?
choices: The Askel eruption was the largest eruption to deposit ash at Maren Bay in the last 9,000 years.
No eruption that occurred before the Askel eruption produced ash that matches the Askel ash in chemical composition.
The sediment layers beneath the ash at Maren Bay were deposited at a steady rate.
No eruption that occurred well after the Askel eruption produced ash that matches the Askel ash in chemical composition.
Ash from the Askel eruption has been identified at several other sites near Maren Bay.
questions.explanation: The argument dates the ash layer by its chemical match to the Askel eruption, so it needs the match not to point to some later source. Negate (D): a much later eruption produced identical ash, so the layer, and the sediment beneath it, could be far younger. (B) is the trap: it uses the same words, but an earlier look-alike eruption would make the layer older, which only helps the conclusion. (A), (C), and (E) aren't needed.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The sediment layers directly beneath the ash in the Maren Bay cliffs were deposited more than about 9,000 years ago.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The ash matches, chemically, the ash from Mount Askel's eruption about 9,000 years ago; an eruption's ash usually has a distinguishable signature; layers below are older than layers above.

breakdown.analysis: 'Usually' distinguishable isn't 'always.' What if another eruption made matching ash? Then it depends which way. If the look-alike eruption was later, the ash could be young and so could the layers under it: the conclusion fails. If it was earlier, the layers are even older: the conclusion is fine. So the argument only needs to rule out a LATER match. Prephrase: no much later eruption produced the same ash.

choices.note: Wrong. The eruption doesn't have to be the biggest for its ash to be identified by chemistry. Negating it does no harm.
choices.negation: The Askel eruption was not the largest eruption to deposit ash at Maren Bay in the last 9,000 years.

choices.note: Tempting. It's word-for-word the right idea, pointed the wrong way in time. If an EARLIER eruption made identical ash, the layer might be older than 9,000 years, and the sediment below it older still. Negating it doesn't hurt the conclusion at all.
choices.negation: Some eruption that occurred before the Askel eruption produced ash that matches the Askel ash in chemical composition.

choices.note: Wrong. Deposit rate matters only if you calculate age from thickness. The argument only claims the lower layers are older than the ash. Negating it does no harm.
choices.negation: The sediment layers beneath the ash at Maren Bay were not deposited at a steady rate.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: some eruption well after Askel's produced matching ash. Then the Maren Bay ash might come from that eruption, and the layers beneath it could be much younger than 9,000 years. The argument falls apart.
choices.negation: Some eruption that occurred well after the Askel eruption produced ash that matches the Askel ash in chemical composition.

choices.note: Wrong. Whether Askel ash shows up elsewhere doesn't affect how old the Maren Bay layers are. Negating it does no harm.
choices.negation: Ash from the Askel eruption has not been identified at several other sites near Maren Bay.

questions.stimulus: Musicologist: Some scholars hold that a song counts as a folk song only if no one knows who composed it. But by that standard, if a letter newly found in an archive revealed who had composed some traditional song, that song would stop being a folk song on the day the letter was read, even though nothing about the song or the way people sing it had changed. Surely what kind of song something is cannot depend on such an accident.
questions.stem: The musicologist's argument proceeds by
choices: offering a more precise definition of a folk song to replace the one that the scholars have proposed
arguing that the scholars' standard is useless because the composers of most folk songs can never be identified
questioning whether research in archives is a reliable means of establishing who composed a given song
citing an actual case in which a song ceased to be regarded as a folk song once its composer was identified
rejecting a standard because, applied to an imagined case, it makes a song's status hinge on a mere discovery
questions.explanation: The musicologist imagines a song whose composer is discovered and shows that the scholars' standard would make it stop being a folk song even though the song itself is unchanged; that result is rejected as absurd, and the standard with it. (E) describes this. (D) is the trap: the case is hypothetical, and the musicologist denies, rather than reports, that the song stopped being a folk song. (A) is wrong because no replacement definition is offered, and (B) and (C) give reasons the musicologist never uses.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The scholars' standard (a folk song is one whose composer is unknown) is wrong.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Under that standard, a song whose composer was discovered would stop being a folk song at the moment of discovery, though the song itself hasn't changed; a song's kind can't depend on such an accident.

breakdown.analysis: Notice the move: 'by that standard...' The musicologist takes the scholars' rule, applies it to a made-up case, and gets a silly result: the song changes category the minute someone reads a letter. Since the result is unacceptable, so is the rule. That's refuting a criterion by showing it gives an absurd answer in a hypothetical case. It's like saying: if 'tall' meant 'taller than everyone in the room,' you'd stop being tall whenever a basketball player walked in. Prephrase: shows the standard has an unacceptable consequence in an imagined case.

choices.note: Tempting, since the musicologist clearly thinks the scholars' definition is wrong. But no replacement is offered. Criticizing a definition isn't the same as proposing a new one.
choices.example: Example of this method: The scholars define a folk song as anonymous; a better definition is a song passed on mainly by ear.

choices.note: Wrong. The musicologist never says the standard can't be applied. The complaint is the opposite: applied to a song, it gives the wrong answer.
choices.example: Example of this method: The standard is useless, since we can almost never learn who wrote a traditional song.

choices.note: Wrong. The musicologist never doubts the archive letter. The argument assumes the composer really was identified; that's what makes the result absurd.
choices.example: Example of this method: Letters in archives are often forged, so we cannot rely on them to identify composers.

choices.note: Tempting, because it borrows the stimulus's words. But two things are off. The case is imagined ('if a letter newly found in an archive revealed...'), not an actual case. And the musicologist doesn't report that the song stopped being regarded as a folk song; the point is that it shouldn't.
choices.example: Example of this method: When the composer of "Willow Lane" was discovered in 1990, collectors dropped it from folk anthologies.

choices.note: CORRECT. The musicologist rejects the scholars' standard by applying it to a hypothetical case and showing it makes the song's classification depend on a discovery rather than on anything about the song.

questions.stimulus: Gray shrikes in the Ostrava Hills impale the insects they catch on thorns before eating them. One grasshopper species common in the hills carries a toxin that breaks down within two days after the insect dies. Shrikes eat most impaled prey within a few hours, but they leave impaled grasshoppers of this species on the thorns for two days or more before eating them. Thus, ______.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: shrikes impale prey on thorns chiefly in order to make toxic prey safe to eat
the toxin carried by these grasshoppers is harmful to most of the bird species that eat them
shrikes would eat more of these grasshoppers if the grasshoppers' toxin broke down more quickly
shrikes in the Ostrava Hills catch more of these grasshoppers than any other kind of prey
the shrikes' practice of impaling prey may help protect them from the grasshoppers' toxin
questions.explanation: Shrikes wait just long enough for the toxin to break down before eating these grasshoppers, so impaling, which lets them store the prey, plausibly protects them from the toxin, as E cautiously states. A overreaches with 'chiefly': shrikes impale all their prey, most of which they eat within hours, so detoxifying cannot be the main purpose. B, C, and D go beyond anything the facts establish.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1) Shrikes impale insects they catch on thorns before eating them; 2) One common grasshopper carries a toxin that breaks down within two days after it dies; 3) Shrikes eat most impaled prey within hours; 4) They leave these grasshoppers impaled for two days or more before eating them.

breakdown.analysis: The facts line up suspiciously well: the toxin breaks down in two days, and shrikes wait two days or more before eating these grasshoppers. So impaling gives them a way to store the toxic prey until it's safe. That's the inference. But careful: shrikes impale everything, and eat most prey within hours, so detox can't be the main reason they impale. Prephrase: impaling may help shrikes avoid the toxin.

choices.note: Wrong. Too strong with 'chiefly.' Shrikes impale all their prey and eat most of it within a few hours, so detoxifying can't be the main purpose. It's one benefit for one species of prey.
Wrong. The facts are only about shrikes and this grasshopper. Nothing tells you about most bird species.
Wrong. Unsupported prediction. Nothing says shrikes are limited by the wait. They might eat exactly as many either way.
Wrong. Nothing about how much of their diet is grasshoppers. 'Common in the hills' isn't 'most-caught prey.'

CORRECT. The hedge ('may help') makes it easy to support. The waiting time matches the toxin's breakdown time, and impaling is what lets them store prey that long. So impaling plausibly protects them from the toxin.

questions.stimulus: Energy analyst: Ten years ago, rooftop solar panels generated 5 percent of the electricity used by households in Velmont. Today they generate 9 percent, and the share supplied by all other sources combined has fallen accordingly. So Velmont households now draw less electricity from sources other than rooftop solar than they did ten years ago.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the energy analyst's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: takes for granted that the share of electricity supplied by rooftop solar panels will keep rising over the next ten years
presumes, without providing justification, that rooftop solar panels generate more electricity in Velmont now than they did ten years ago
treats the households that have installed rooftop solar panels as representative of all of the households in Velmont
overlooks the possibility that Velmont households use considerably more electricity in total than they did ten years ago
fails to consider whether the electricity supplied by sources other than rooftop solar has become cheaper or more costly
questions.explanation: The non-solar share fell from 95 to 91 percent, but if total household use grew by more than about 4.4 percent, the amount drawn from other sources actually rose; (D) names the overlooked growth in the total. (B) is the trap: it is about the amount of solar power, which the argument neither needs nor assumes. (A) misreads the conclusion as a prediction, (C) invents a sample, and (E) raises cost, which the conclusion never mentions.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Velmont households now draw less electricity from non-solar sources than ten years ago.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Rooftop solar's share of household electricity rose from 5 to 9 percent, so the share from all other sources fell (95 to 91 percent).

breakdown.analysis: Share went down, so amount went down? Not if the pie got bigger. Worked example: ten years ago households used 100 units, 95 from non-solar. Today they use 120 units; 91 percent of 120 is about 109 non-solar units. That's more, not less. Percent isn't amount. Prephrase: the argument ignores that total use may have grown.

choices.note: Wrong. The conclusion is about now, not the next ten years. No prediction is made.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Solar has grown every year for a decade, so it will supply half our power within ten more years.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like the percent-versus-amount issue. But it's about the wrong amount. The conclusion concerns non-solar electricity, and the argument needs no claim about how much solar power is produced. If anything, solar output rising is likely, not a hidden flaw.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Solar supplies a bigger share than before, so it obviously supplies more kilowatt-hours than before.

choices.note: Wrong. The figures cover all Velmont households, not a sample of solar owners. There's no generalization from a subgroup.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Households with solar panels cut their grid use, so every household in town must have cut its grid use.

choices.note: CORRECT. That's the gap. A smaller share of a larger total can be a larger amount. If households use enough more electricity overall, the non-solar amount went up even though its share fell.
Wrong. Cost is a different dimension. The conclusion is about how much electricity is drawn, not what it costs.

questions.stimulus: Principal: Every course in Fairview High School's new humanities sequence should count toward the school's information-literacy requirement. After all, any course that requires students to complete a substantial independent research project develops students' ability to evaluate sources, and every course in the new sequence requires such a project.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the principal's argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Only courses that develop students' ability to evaluate sources should be counted toward the school's information-literacy requirement.
Any course that develops students' ability to evaluate sources should count toward the school's information-literacy requirement.
Students who complete a substantial independent research project tend to evaluate sources better than students who do not.
Most courses that develop students' ability to evaluate sources should count toward the school's information-literacy requirement.
Most of the courses offered outside the new humanities sequence do not develop students' ability to evaluate sources.
questions.explanation: The premises establish that every course in the sequence develops students' ability to evaluate sources; (B) links that property to counting toward the requirement, so the conclusion follows. (A) is the trap: it reverses the needed conditional, making source evaluation necessary for counting rather than sufficient. (D) has the right direction but only 'most,' so the sequence's courses could be among the exceptions; (C) and (E) never connect the courses to the requirement.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Every course in the new humanities sequence should count toward the information-literacy requirement.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Research-project course → develops source evaluation; every sequence course requires a research project.

breakdown.analysis: Map the chain. Sequence course → research project → develops source evaluation. The conclusion jumps to → should count. The missing link: develops source evaluation → should count. Full chain: sequence course → project → source evaluation → counts. Like: all my roommates are nurses, all nurses work nights, so my roommates should get the night-shift discount. You need 'every night worker gets the discount.'

choices.note: Tempting, because it uses all the right terms. But it runs the wrong way: counts → develops source evaluation. That makes source evaluation necessary for counting, not enough for it. The sequence's courses meet a requirement for counting; that doesn't make them count.
CORRECT. Develops source evaluation → should count. Every sequence course develops source evaluation, so every one should count. The chain is complete.
Wrong. This supports the premise about research projects. It says nothing about what should count toward the requirement.
Tempting: right direction, wrong strength. 'Most' leaves room for the sequence's courses to be the exceptions. A sufficient assumption has to guarantee every one of them, and 'most' can't.
Wrong. Other courses are irrelevant. The conclusion is only about the courses in the new sequence.

questions.stimulus: For decades, groundwater has been pumped heavily for irrigation in the Halden Valley, and as a result the land surface over most of the valley has sunk by more than a meter. In recent years, pumping has continued at the same rate and the water table has kept falling just as fast as before, yet the land has been sinking much more slowly than it did earlier.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: In most of the valley, the underground layers that compress most readily when groundwater is withdrawn have already been compressed nearly to their limit.
Land sinks when the removal of groundwater allows underground layers of fine clay to compact under the weight of the material above them.
Many new buildings have been constructed in the valley in recent years, adding to the weight bearing down on the layers beneath.
In other irrigated valleys of the region, the land has also been sinking more slowly in recent years than it did earlier.
In a neighboring valley where far less groundwater is pumped, the land has sunk by only a few centimeters in total.
questions.explanation: The puzzle is why unchanged pumping and an equally fast-falling water table now produce less sinking. (A) explains it: the layers that compress easily have nearly finished compressing, so the same withdrawal yields little further sinking. (B) is the trap: it explains why pumping causes sinking at all but not why the sinking has slowed. (C) deepens the puzzle, (D) only shows the puzzle is widespread, and (E) confirms that pumping causes sinking.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Pumping and the falling water table continue exactly as before, but the land is sinking much more slowly.

breakdown.analysis: Same cause, weaker effect. So something about the ground itself must have changed. Prephrase: whatever compacts has mostly already compacted. Think of squeezing a sponge: the first squeezes flatten it a lot, but once it's squashed, squeezing just as hard barely changes it. Watch for the answer that explains why sinking happens at all; that's not the question.

choices.note: CORRECT. The squashed sponge. The layers that compress when water is pulled out are nearly as compressed as they can get, so the same pumping produces little more sinking. Both facts fit.
Tempting, because it's the right mechanism. But it explains why pumping makes land sink, which nobody doubted. It says nothing about why the same pumping now causes less sinking.
Wrong. More weight on the layers should make the land sink faster, not slower. This deepens the puzzle.
Wrong. Showing that other valleys have the same puzzle doesn't solve it. It just makes it bigger.
Wrong. This confirms that heavy pumping causes sinking. It doesn't explain the recent slowdown in the Halden Valley.

questions.stimulus: Columnist: The Dalby Cannery cut its workers' hourly wages last month, citing recent losses. But two years ago, when the workers agreed to forgo a scheduled raise, the owners promised not to reduce wages as long as the cannery's most recent full year had been profitable. The cannery made a profit last year, its most recent full year, despite its losses in recent months. So the wage cut was unjustified.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, would most help to justify the columnist's argument?
choices: Workers who forgo a scheduled raise are entitled to have it restored as soon as their employer returns to profitability.
Those who give up a benefit in exchange for an assurance are entitled to have the assurance honored whenever the circumstances it specifies obtain.
Wage reductions are justified only when they are genuinely needed to keep a company from going out of business.
An employer's promise to its workers remains binding only for as long as the employer's financial circumstances stay substantially the same.
Promises that employers make during labor negotiations are binding only if they have been put in writing.
questions.explanation: The columnist's case is that the workers gave up a raise for a promise, and the promise's condition (a profitable most recent year) held, so the cut broke the promise; (B) states that principle in general terms. (A) has the right condition but the wrong verdict (restoring the raise, not barring a cut). (C) can't reach the conclusion because we don't know whether the cut was needed for survival, (D) points the other way, and (E) depends on a fact the columnist never gives.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The wage cut was unjustified.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Workers gave up a raise; in return the owners promised no wage cut while the most recent full year was profitable; last year was profitable.

breakdown.analysis: This is about a deal. The workers gave something up; the owners promised something back; the promise's condition was met. A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says. Prephrase: if you give something up in exchange for a promise, and the promise's condition holds, you're owed what was promised. The right answer may describe the deal in abstract words, so match the pieces: benefit given up = the raise, assurance = the promise, circumstances = a profitable year.

choices.note: Tempting, because the condition matches: the cannery is profitable. But the verdict is wrong. It's about getting the raise back, not about whether wages may be cut.

CORRECT. Abstract, but it fits: the workers gave up a benefit (the raise) for an assurance (no cuts), and the circumstances the assurance names (a profitable latest year) hold. So the workers were owed no cut, and cutting was unjustified.
Wrong. We don't know whether the cut was needed to keep the cannery open; it did have recent losses. So this can't establish that the cut was unjustified.
Wrong direction. The cannery's finances did change (recent losses), so this principle would release the owners from the promise. It helps the cannery.
Wrong. We aren't told whether the promise was written. If it wasn't, this would undercut the columnist.

questions.stimulus: After Dunmore County raised its minimum wage last year, employment at the county's restaurants did not decline. However, the average number of hours worked per restaurant employee fell by about 10 percent, and restaurants posted fewer job openings than in previous years. Over the same period, the rate at which restaurant employees quit their jobs dropped sharply.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: The increase in the minimum wage is what caused the county's restaurants to reduce the hours their employees worked.
Fewer employees leaving their jobs may account for part of the decline in the restaurants' job openings.
Restaurant employees in Dunmore County earned less money in total last year than they had the year before.
The number of people employed at the county's restaurants rose after the minimum wage was increased.
Restaurants that reduced their employees' hours posted fewer job openings than other restaurants did.
questions.explanation: Job openings arise largely when workers leave, so a sharp drop in quitting gives a plausible partial explanation for fewer openings; (B)'s hedged claim is well supported. (A) is the tempting trap, but the facts show only that hours fell after the wage rose, not that the wage increase caused it. (C) cannot be determined without knowing how much hourly pay rose, (D) goes beyond 'did not decline,' and (E) compares restaurants the facts never distinguish.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1) After the minimum wage rose, restaurant employment did not decline; 2) Average hours per employee fell about 10 percent; 3) Restaurants posted fewer job openings than in previous years; 4) The rate at which restaurant employees quit dropped sharply.

breakdown.analysis: No conclusion here, so look for the answer the facts back up without stretching. Think about where job openings come from: mostly from people leaving. If far fewer people quit, there are fewer spots to fill, so fewer openings. That's a solid, hedged inference. Be suspicious of anything claiming causation from the wage increase; the facts only give timing.

choices.note: Wrong. Tempting, but it's causal. The facts say hours fell after the wage rose, not because of it. Something else could have cut hours. Timing isn't proof.
CORRECT. The hedge ('may account for part of') makes this easy to support. Fewer people quitting means fewer vacancies to fill, which plausibly explains some of the drop in openings.
Wrong. Hours fell 10 percent, but hourly pay rose by an unknown amount. If the wage went up 20 percent, total pay could still rise. Can't be determined.
Wrong. 'Did not decline' means stayed the same or rose. You can't conclude it rose. Watch that shift.
Wrong. The facts give county-wide averages and never break restaurants into groups. This comparison has no support.

questions.stimulus: Parks official: Critics claim that replacing the lawn in Orchard Square with native meadow plants has made the square less popular, noting that it now draws fewer visitors. But in a survey posted on the square's information board this summer, 85 percent of the 300 respondents said they approve of the meadow. Clearly, then, the meadow is popular with the public, and the drop in visitors must have some other cause.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the parks official's argument?
choices: A survey conducted before the meadow was planted found that 80 percent of respondents approved of the square's lawn.
Many of the square's former regular visitors now spend their time instead at a nearby park that kept its lawn.
Some of the people who responded to the survey were tourists visiting the city for the first time.
Construction on a street bordering the square has made the square harder to reach for much of this year.
The meadow requires more frequent maintenance by park staff than the lawn did, which has raised the labor costs.
questions.explanation: The survey reached only people who still come to the square and read its board. (B) shows that many former regulars left for a park that kept its lawn, which suggests they dislike the meadow and that the survey missed them, and also points to the meadow as the cause of the drop. (A) and (C) look like sample problems but don't show the respondents misrepresent the public's view of the meadow; (D) strengthens by offering another cause; (E) is about cost, not popularity.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The meadow is popular with the public, and the drop in visitors has some other cause.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 85 percent of 300 respondents to a survey posted on the square's own board approve of the meadow.

breakdown.analysis: Who took the survey? People standing in the square reading its board. Those are the people who still come. The people who stopped coming, the ones most likely to dislike the change, never saw it. It's like surveying diners inside a restaurant about its new menu. We want an answer showing the missing people dislike the meadow. Most students hunt for an answer that names the survey; the right one doesn't. It just tells you where the lost visitors went and, by implication, why.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's another survey and suggests people liked the lawn. But people can like a lawn and still like the meadow. It doesn't show that the meadow is unpopular now.

CORRECT. Former regulars moved to a park that kept its lawn. That suggests they left because of the meadow, and it means the survey on the square's board couldn't reach them. The 85 percent doesn't represent the public, and the 'other cause' looks doubtful.
Tempting, because it sounds like a biased sample. But tourists are members of the public too, and nothing suggests they favor the meadow more than residents do. Interesting, but not damaging.
Wrong direction. Road construction is exactly the kind of 'other cause' the official needs. This strengthens the argument.
Wrong dimension. Cost is not popularity. This might support the critics' larger complaint, but it doesn't touch the claim that the public likes the meadow.

questions.stimulus: Journal editor: Several readers have asked us to retract Dr. Imre Salo's paper on soil fungi because a later study failed to reproduce its main result. We will not do so. Nothing suggests that Salo misreported his data or erred in analyzing them, and the failure of one later study, however careful, does not show that his paper contains a mistake.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the editor's position?
choices: A journal should retract a paper only if readers have raised doubts about it and a later study has failed to reproduce its main result.
Any paper whose main result has been reproduced by later studies should remain in the published record.
A paper whose data were misreported should be retracted even if its main result is later reproduced by other researchers.
When a later study fails to reproduce a published result, the journal should print a notice informing its readers of the failure.
Unless there is some indication that a paper's findings were misrepresented or wrongly derived, the paper should remain in the published record.
questions.explanation: The editor refuses to retract because there is no sign that the data were misreported or the analysis was wrong. (E) says that without such a sign a paper stays in the record, which yields the editor's position. (A) is the trap: both of its conditions are met here, but they are only necessary for retraction, so meeting them settles nothing. (B) applies to reproduced results, which this isn't; (C) applies only to misreported data; (D) prescribes a notice, not a decision about retraction.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The journal will not (and should not) retract Salo's paper.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Nothing suggests Salo misreported data or made an analysis error; one failed replication does not show the paper contains a mistake.

breakdown.analysis: We need a rule whose trigger matches the facts and whose verdict is 'don't retract.' The facts: no sign of misreporting, no sign of an analysis error, one failed replication. Prephrase: no evidence of misreporting or error → don't retract. The right answer says this in disguise: 'misrepresented' = misreported, 'wrongly derived' = analysis error, 'remain in the published record' = not retracted. Most students pick (A) because both of its conditions (readers' doubts, failed replication) are true here. But it's an 'only if' rule: those conditions are necessary for retraction. Meeting a necessary condition doesn't tell you what to do. A rule that says 'retract only if X' can never justify 'don't retract' when X is true.

choices.note: Tempting, because both conditions match the facts. But 'only if' makes them requirements for retracting, not reasons against it. With both met, the rule permits retraction and gives no verdict either way.
Wrong. This applies to papers whose results were reproduced. Salo's wasn't, so the rule says nothing about his paper.
Wrong. This tells you when to retract, and its condition (misreported data) isn't met. A rule about when to retract can't, by itself, tell you not to.
Wrong verdict. It prescribes printing a notice, which is consistent with retracting or not retracting. It doesn't support refusing to retract.
CORRECT. No indication of misrepresentation or faulty derivation → the paper stays. The editor says nothing suggests misreporting or analysis errors, so the paper stays: no retraction.

questions.stimulus: Every film shown at the Corvo Festival this year was chosen by the festival's selection jury, and the jury chose no film that had already been released commercially. The Long Field has already been released commercially, so it was not shown at the Corvo Festival this year.
questions.stem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following arguments is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: Every car sold at Henley Motors is inspected by Pratt, and Pratt inspects no car that has more than 100,000 miles on it. So the sedan Pratt inspected last week has no more than 100,000 miles on it.
The Birchwood Café's head chef prepares no dish with peanuts, and only dishes the head chef prepares appear on the café's lunch menu. The café's satay has peanuts, so it is not on that menu.

Every painting in the east gallery was donated by Ames, and Ames donated no painting that was made before 1900. The Tolland portrait was made before 1900, so it was not one of the paintings Ames donated.
Every member of the choir auditioned for the director, and the director turned away no one who could read music. Since Lin can read music, it follows that Lin must be a member of the choir.

Every book in the reading room was approved by the librarian, and the librarian approves only those books that are in good condition. This atlas is in good condition, so it must be in the reading room.
questions.explanation: The argument chains two rules (shown at the festival → chosen by the jury → not released commercially) and, from an item that lacks the final property, concludes by contrapositive that it lacks the first: it was not shown. (B) does the same with its rules stated in a different order and with 'only': the satay contains peanuts, so the chef did not prepare it, so it is not on the menu. (C) is the trap: its first sentence copies the stimulus's form, but it stops at the middle term and never uses the gallery premise. (A) reasons forward from the middle term, and (D) and (E) reverse the conditionals.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Long Field was not shown at the Corvo Festival this year.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Every film shown was chosen by the jury; the jury chose no film already released commercially; The Long Field was already released commercially.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: A → B; B → not C; this item is C; so it is not B, and so not A.

breakdown.analysis: Diagram it. Shown → chosen by jury → not released. The Long Field is released, so by contrapositive: not chosen, and so not shown. The conclusion lands on the FIRST term of the chain. Find the answer that runs the whole chain backward to the first term. Most students pick (C) because its first sentence is a carbon copy: 'Every … was … by Ames, and Ames … no …'. It fails because it concludes only that Ames didn't donate the portrait. That's the middle term; the gallery premise does no work. Like proving a dish wasn't cooked by the chef and stopping there, never saying it's not on the menu. (B) hides because it puts the second rule first and phrases the first one with 'only': only chef-prepared dishes are on the menu means on menu → chef prepared.

choices.note: Wrong. This starts from the middle term (Pratt inspected it) and runs forward to a conclusion. It never uses the Henley premise and never denies anything by contrapositive.

CORRECT. On menu → chef prepared ('only'); chef prepared → no peanuts. The satay has peanuts, so the chef didn't prepare it, so it's not on the menu. Same two-step contrapositive back to the first term.

Tempting. It looks the most like the stimulus. But it stops halfway: not donated by Ames. It never concludes the portrait isn't in the east gallery, so the first premise is idle. Half the chain is not the same pattern.
Wrong. 'Turned away no one who could read music' doesn't mean everyone who reads music joined. It reverses the conditional: from the condition to membership.
Wrong. Reading room → good condition. Being in good condition doesn't put the atlas in the reading room. Reversed conditional.

questions.stimulus: Some historians argue that the Brennock Canal was built mainly to carry coal, pointing out that coal made up most of its cargo in the decades after it opened. But the canal company's charter, drafted before the region's large coal seams had been discovered, names only grain and timber as the cargo the canal was meant to serve. The coal traffic, then, reflects a use that arose later, and it tells us nothing about why the canal was built.
questions.stem: The claim that coal made up most of the canal's cargo in the decades after it opened plays which one of the following roles in the argument?
choices: It is a claim that the argument attempts to show is false by appealing to the contents of the canal company's charter.
It is a premise of the historians' argument that the argument concedes lends their view some support but holds is outweighed by the charter.
It is a premise that the argument uses, together with the charter's contents, to establish the purpose for which the canal was built.
It is a premise of an opposing argument that the argument accepts as accurate but contends is irrelevant to the matter in dispute.
It is the conclusion of the historians' argument, which the argument rejects as resting on a misreading of the charter.
questions.explanation: The historians cite the coal traffic as evidence that the canal was built for coal. The author accepts that coal dominated the cargo but argues that it reflects a later use and tells us nothing about the canal's purpose; (D) captures both halves. (B) is the trap: the author doesn't weigh the coal evidence against the charter but denies it has any bearing. (A) has the author disputing a fact the author grants, (C) misassigns the support, and (E) confuses the historians' evidence with their conclusion.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The coal traffic reflects a later use and tells us nothing about why the canal was built (so the historians are wrong).

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The charter, written before the coal seams were found, names only grain and timber as the intended cargo.

breakdown.analysis: Who says coal made up most of the cargo? The historians, as their evidence. Does the author dispute it? No: 'The coal traffic, then, reflects a use that arose later' treats the traffic as real. The author's fight is over what it shows: 'nothing about why the canal was built.' So the claim is the other side's premise, granted as true, but called irrelevant. Most students pick (B) because concede-then-outweigh is such a common structure. It fails because the author doesn't say the coal evidence is weaker than the charter; the author says it isn't evidence of purpose at all. 'Outweighed' and 'irrelevant' are different roles.

choices.note: Wrong. The author never says coal didn't dominate the cargo. The author disputes the historians' conclusion, not this fact.

Tempting. It gets the owner (the historians) and the concession right. But the author doesn't concede the coal traffic gives the historians' view 'some support'; the author says it tells us nothing about the canal's purpose. That's irrelevance, not being outweighed.
Wrong. The author's case about the canal's purpose rests on the charter alone. The coal claim isn't used to support it; it's set aside.

CORRECT. It's the historians' premise (an opposing argument), the author grants it ('reflects a use that arose later' treats it as true), and the author says it 'tells us nothing about why the canal was built': irrelevant to the dispute.
Wrong. The historians' conclusion is that the canal was built mainly for coal. The coal-cargo claim is their evidence for it, not the conclusion itself.

questions.stimulus: Records show that the silent film The Lantern Keeper was shown in only three cities during its original release, and few reviews of it were published. Yet its distinctive camera techniques appear in dozens of films by directors who began working in the years just after its release. These directors, then, must have seen The Lantern Keeper.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
choices: At least some of the directors who used the techniques lived in or visited one of the three cities during the film's original release.
The few reviews of The Lantern Keeper that were published at the time singled out its camera techniques for praise.
None of the directors who used the techniques acquired them solely by studying the films of other directors who used them.
The directors who used the techniques were, on the whole, more innovative than most other directors working at the time.
The Lantern Keeper was seen by more people than the surviving records of its original release indicate.
questions.explanation: The argument infers that every director who used the techniques must have seen the film, which requires that the techniques could not reach them by another route. Dozens of films used them, so a later director could have picked them up from an earlier imitator. Negate (C): some director learned the techniques only from other directors' films, and that director need not have seen The Lantern Keeper. (A) is the trap: it looks like a modest access assumption, but the argument never says the directors saw the film during its original release, so they could have seen it later. (E), (B), and (D) are not required.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The directors whose films use The Lantern Keeper's camera techniques must have seen The Lantern Keeper.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The film showed in only three cities in its original release and got few reviews; its distinctive techniques appear in dozens of films by directors who started soon after.

breakdown.analysis: 'Must have seen' is very strong. It takes for granted that using the techniques means you saw the original. But dozens of films used them. Couldn't a director have copied the techniques from one of those other films? Like a cover band learning a song from another cover band, never hearing the original. We need an answer that rules out second-hand learning. Most students pick (A) because it looks like the classic hedged NA answer about access to the film. It fails because the argument never says the directors saw the film during its original release; the three-city limit applies only to that run, and they could have seen it later. (C) hides because it's about other directors' films, which the stimulus never mentions, and because it's worded strongly ('none'). It has to be: the conclusion covers every one of 'these directors.'

choices.note: Tempting. 'At least some' sounds like a safe necessary assumption. But the directors could have seen the film after its original release, at a later screening or from a print. Negate it and the argument survives.
choices.negation: None of the directors who used the techniques lived in or visited one of the three cities during the film's original release.

choices.note: Wrong. What reviewers praised doesn't matter. The directors could have seen the film no matter what the reviews said. Negating it does no damage.
choices.negation: The few reviews published at the time did not all single out the film's camera techniques for praise.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: some director learned the techniques only from imitators' films. That director needn't have seen The Lantern Keeper, so 'these directors must have seen it' fails.
choices.negation: At least one of the directors who used the techniques acquired them solely by studying the films of other directors who used them.

choices.note: Wrong. How innovative the directors were is beside the point. Negating it changes nothing about whether they saw the film.
choices.negation: The directors who used the techniques were not, on the whole, more innovative than most other directors of the time.

choices.note: Wrong. It would help, but it isn't required. Even if the records are accurate, the directors could be among the people who saw the film. Negating it doesn't break the argument.
choices.negation: The Lantern Keeper was not seen by more people than the surviving records of its original release indicate.

questions.stimulus: Conservationist: Any bird species in the Pellam Islands whose nests are within reach of the introduced rats is in danger of local extinction unless it breeds more than once a year. Every bird species in danger of local extinction there should be included in the new captive-breeding program. The Pellam rail nests only on the ground, where the rats can reach its nests. So the Pellam rail should be included in the captive-breeding program.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the conservationist's argument can be properly drawn if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Only bird species whose nests are within reach of the rats should be included in the new captive-breeding program.
The Pellam rail breeds less often than any other bird species in the Pellam Islands whose nests the rats can reach.
Any bird species that breeds only once a year is in danger of local extinction if rats can reach its nests.
Pellam bird species that breed more than once a year all nest at least partly off the ground.
Every bird species in the Pellam Islands that nests only on the ground breeds more than once a year.
questions.explanation: The rail's nests are within the rats' reach, so it is in danger, and belongs in the program, unless it breeds more than once a year; the argument needs to rule that out. (D), by contrapositive, says a species that nests only on the ground does not breed more than once a year, which completes the chain. (B) is the trap: breeding less often than every other exposed species is a relative claim and is compatible with breeding twice a year. (C) restates part of the first rule, (A) is irrelevant, and (E) would defeat the conclusion.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Pellam rail should be included in the captive-breeding program.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Nests within rats' reach AND not breeding more than once a year → in danger; in danger → should be in the program; the rail nests only on the ground, within the rats' reach.

breakdown.analysis: Build the chain. Rats can reach the nests → in danger UNLESS the species breeds more than once a year. In danger → program. We know the rail's nests are reachable. What's missing? That the rail does NOT breed more than once a year. Find the answer that guarantees it. (D) does it in contrapositive form: breeds more than once a year → nests at least partly off the ground. Contrapositive: nests only on the ground → doesn't breed more than once a year. The rail nests only on the ground. Done. Most students pick (B) because 'breeds less often than any other' sounds like 'breeds rarely.' It fails because it's relative. If every other exposed species breeds three times a year, the rail could breed twice and escape the danger rule. Watch the switch from a relative word (less often) to an absolute one (not more than once).

choices.note: Wrong. This limits who else can be included. It says nothing about whether the rail breeds more than once a year, which is the missing link.

Tempting. It sounds like the rail barely breeds. But 'less often than the others' is relative. The rail could still breed twice a year if the others breed more, and then the danger rule doesn't apply.
Wrong. This restates part of the first rule. It doesn't tell you how often the rail breeds, so the chain still has a gap.
CORRECT. Contrapositive: nests only on the ground → does not breed more than once a year. The rail nests only on the ground, so it's in danger and belongs in the program.
Wrong. Opposite. If ground-only nesters breed more than once a year, the rail escapes the danger rule and the conclusion doesn't follow.

questions.stimulus: For a Quarrow apple seedling to bear fruit in its third year, it must be grafted onto dwarf rootstock and planted where it gets full sun. Every seedling in Tess Rowan's new orchard row was grafted onto dwarf rootstock, and the row faces south with no shade at all. So the seedlings in that row will bear fruit in their third year.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits a flawed pattern of reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?
choices: No orchestra will be considered for the festival's opening night unless it has played at the festival before and has a board-approved conductor. The Tamberly Orchestra has played there twice and has such a conductor, so it will be considered.

Any runner who finishes the qualifying race in under three hours and has paid the entry fee will be admitted to the championship. Dana paid the fee but finished in over three hours, so she will not be admitted to the championship.

A volunteer may handle the rare maps in the city archive only if she has completed conservation training and been approved by the curator. Petra has not been approved by the curator, so she may not handle the rare maps.

Any tenant at the Hesketh Building who gives sixty days' notice and leaves the unit undamaged gets the full deposit back. The Wrexleys gave sixty days' notice and left their unit undamaged, so they will get their full security deposit back.

Each of the four members of the Pindar Quartet is an accomplished soloist who has won national competitions. So the Pindar Quartet must itself be an accomplished ensemble, one that would win national competitions for quartets.
questions.explanation: 'Must be grafted ... and planted in full sun' states two necessary conditions for third-year fruit; the argument shows both are met and concludes the fruit will come, treating necessary conditions as sufficient. (A) does the same in 'no ... unless' form: two requirements for consideration are met, so consideration is concluded. (D) is the trap: it matches the surface (two conditions met, so the result), but its conditions are stated as sufficient, so it is valid. (C) is a valid use of 'only if,' (B) negates a sufficient condition (a different flaw), and (E) argues from parts to whole.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The seedlings in Rowan's row will bear fruit in their third year.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Third-year fruit requires dwarf rootstock and full sun; the row has both.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Result → A and B (A and B are required); A and B are present; so the result will happen. Necessary conditions treated as sufficient.

breakdown.analysis: 'Must be grafted and planted in full sun' sounds like a recipe, but it's only a list of requirements. Fruit → grafted AND full sun. Meeting the requirements doesn't guarantee fruit; the tree could still get blight or a bad frost. It's like saying you must have a ticket to get into the concert, I have a ticket, so I'll get in (the show could be cancelled). Find the answer where two requirements are met and the result is concluded. 'No X unless A and B' means X → A and B, same as 'must.' Most students pick (D) because it looks identical: two conditions met, so the result. It fails because its rule says the conditions are enough ('any tenant who ... gets'), so the argument is valid. A flawed original needs a flawed match.

choices.note: CORRECT. 'No orchestra will be considered unless it has played there and has an approved conductor' = considered → played AND approved conductor. Those are requirements. Tamberly meets both, and the argument concludes it will be considered. Same necessary-as-sufficient error.

Wrong. This rule gives sufficient conditions, and Dana fails one, so the argument concludes she won't be admitted. That's a different error: negating a sufficient condition. It's flawed, but not in the same way.
Wrong. 'Only if' gives necessary conditions, and Petra fails one, so she may not handle the maps. That's a valid inference. Tempting because it shares the 'only if ... and ...' shape.

Tempting. Same surface: two conditions met, so the result. But 'any tenant who gives notice and leaves the unit undamaged gets the deposit back' makes the conditions sufficient. The reasoning is valid, so it can't match a flawed original.
Wrong. This goes from qualities of the members to qualities of the group, a part-to-whole flaw. No conditional rule at all.

questions.stimulus: Historian: The unsigned pamphlet denouncing Valtria's salt tax has long been credited to the merchant Aldo Ferrant. But the pamphlet contains, word for word, a long passage that also appears in a speech first delivered and printed in 1794, the year after Ferrant's death. So Ferrant cannot have written the pamphlet, at least in the form in which it survives.
questions.stem: The historian's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?
choices: The version of the pamphlet that survives today is identical to the version that first circulated in Valtria.
No one other than the speech's author knew the wording of the speech before it was delivered.
Ferrant was not the only merchant in Valtria who publicly opposed the salt tax.
The pamphlet was not written by someone who wished to have it mistaken for Ferrant's work.
The passage that appears in the speech was not taken by the speech's author from the pamphlet.
questions.explanation: The historian assumes the pamphlet borrowed the passage from the 1794 speech, which would date the pamphlet after Ferrant's death. But the borrowing could have run the other way: the speaker could have copied an older pamphlet. Negate (E) and Ferrant could have written the pamphlet before 1793. (A) is the trap: the conclusion already concedes that the surviving form may differ from the original ('at least in the form in which it survives'). (B) is too strong, and (C) and (D) aren't needed.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Ferrant cannot have written the pamphlet, at least in its surviving form.

setup.label: Reasoning
