setup.text: The pamphlet shares a long passage, word for word, with a speech first delivered and printed in 1794; Ferrant died in 1793.

breakdown.analysis: The passage appears in both texts. The historian treats that as proof the pamphlet copied the speech. But who copied whom? If the speaker lifted the passage from an older pamphlet, the pamphlet could date from Ferrant's lifetime and the 1794 date tells you nothing. It's like finding the same joke in your friend's essay and in a comedian's new special: you can't tell your friend stole it until you know the comedian didn't steal it from your friend. Prephrase: the speech didn't take the passage from the pamphlet. Most students pick (A) because a changed later version seems like an obvious hole. It fails because the historian already covered it: 'at least in the form in which it survives.' The conclusion is only about the surviving form, so whether that form matches the original doesn't matter. Note too that 'first delivered' in 1794 rules out Ferrant hearing the speech earlier.

choices.note: Tempting. It looks like a gap: what if the pamphlet was revised later? But the conclusion is limited to 'the form in which it survives.' Negate this and the surviving form differs from the original, which fits the conclusion fine.
choices.negation: The version of the pamphlet that survives today is not identical to the version that first circulated in Valtria.

choices.note: Too strong. The argument needs, at most, that Ferrant didn't know the wording early. Negate it and someone besides the author knew the wording beforehand, perhaps a secretary. That someone needn't be Ferrant, so the argument survives.
choices.negation: Someone other than the speech's author knew the wording of the speech before it was delivered.

choices.note: Wrong. Whether others opposed the tax bears on who else might have written it, not on whether Ferrant could have. Negate it and Ferrant was the only opponent; the dating evidence still rules him out.
choices.negation: Ferrant was the only merchant in Valtria who publicly opposed the salt tax.

choices.note: Wrong. An imitator writing the pamphlet would fit the conclusion that Ferrant didn't write it. Negating it does no harm.
choices.negation: The pamphlet was written by someone who wished to have it mistaken for Ferrant's work.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the speech's author took the passage from the pamphlet. Then the pamphlet came first, could easily predate 1793, and Ferrant could have written it. The argument collapses.
choices.negation: The passage that appears in the speech was taken by the speech's author from the pamphlet.

questions.stimulus: Granite boulders scattered across the Tamsin Plain are of a type found in place only in the Dovre Mountains, 200 kilometers to the north. Geologists know of only two processes able to carry boulders that far: glaciers and catastrophic floods. Boulders carried by floods are rounded and smoothed, whereas boulders carried by glaciers typically keep sharp edges and often bear parallel scratches. Most of the Dovre granite boulders on the plain have sharp edges, though a few are rounded.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: The rounded boulders on the Tamsin Plain were carried there by catastrophic floods.
All of the Dovre granite boulders on the Tamsin Plain were carried there by a single glacier.
Most of the Dovre granite boulders on the Tamsin Plain bear parallel scratches.
At least some of the Dovre granite boulders on the Tamsin Plain were carried there by glaciers.
No catastrophic flood has ever swept from the Dovre Mountains to the Tamsin Plain.
questions.explanation: Flood-carried boulders are rounded, so the many sharp-edged boulders could not have come by flood; since only glaciers and floods could carry them, those boulders were carried by glaciers, as (D) says. (A) is the tempting trap: glacier-carried boulders only 'typically' keep sharp edges, so the few rounded ones could also have arrived by glacier. (B) and (E) ignore the rounded boulders' uncertain origin, and (C) overstates 'often bear' scratches.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1) Granite boulders on the Tamsin Plain come only from the Dovre Mountains, 200 km away; 2) Only glaciers and catastrophic floods can carry boulders that far; 3) Flood-carried boulders are rounded and smoothed; 4) Glacier-carried boulders typically keep sharp edges and often have parallel scratches; 5) Most of the plain's boulders are sharp-edged; a few are rounded.

breakdown.analysis: Use the strict rule, not the loose one. Floods → rounded. Contrapositive: sharp-edged → not carried by flood. Only two options exist, so sharp-edged → glacier. Most boulders are sharp, so at least some (in fact most) came by glacier. The rounded ones are a mystery: glacier boulders only 'typically' stay sharp, so a rounded one could have come either way.

choices.note: Wrong. The trap. Floods → rounded doesn't give you rounded → flood. Glacier boulders only 'typically' keep sharp edges, so some rounded ones might have come by glacier too.
Wrong. Too strong twice over. The rounded boulders could have come by flood, and nothing says only one glacier was involved.
Wrong. Glacier boulders 'often' bear scratches, not usually. You can't get to 'most' from 'often.'
CORRECT. Floods always round boulders, so the sharp-edged ones didn't come by flood. With only two possible carriers, they came by glacier. 'At least some' is easily supported.
Wrong. The rounded boulders may well have come by flood. Nothing rules a flood out.

questions.stimulus: Economist: Two years after the town of Ashby began requiring employers to list salary ranges in job postings, the gap between the average starting salaries of men and women hired by Ashby firms had narrowed considerably. The requirement probably narrowed the gap by giving applicants, many of whom had previously had little idea what a position paid, a firmer basis for negotiating their pay.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the economist's argument?
choices: Before the requirement took effect, surveys found that many job applicants in Ashby had little idea what the positions they sought paid.
Some Ashby employers had already been listing salary ranges in their job postings before the requirement took effect.
The narrowing was concentrated in occupations in which starting pay is usually settled by bargaining rather than set by a fixed scale.
Women hired by Ashby firms since the requirement took effect have, on average, more work experience than women hired before it.
Since the requirement took effect, Ashby firms have hired more women than before for positions whose postings list salary ranges.
questions.explanation: The economist claims the requirement narrowed the gap by improving applicants' negotiating position. (C) shows the narrowing happened where negotiation sets pay and not where a fixed scale does, which is just what that mechanism predicts. (A) is the trap: it confirms a fact the economist already asserts but does nothing to link the requirement to the narrowing. (B) weakens slightly, (D) offers an alternative cause, and (E) concerns hiring counts, not starting pay.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The salary-range requirement probably narrowed the starting-salary gap by giving applicants a firmer basis for negotiating.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Two years after the requirement began, the gap between men's and women's average starting salaries had narrowed considerably; many applicants had previously known little about pay.

breakdown.analysis: Two claims here: the requirement caused the narrowing, and it did so through negotiation. How could we test the mechanism? If negotiation is the channel, the gap should shrink where pay is negotiated and not where it's fixed. An answer showing that pattern supports both the cause and the 'how.' It's like testing whether a new study guide raised scores: if scores rose only on the topics the guide covers, the guide gets the credit. Most students pick (A) because it sounds like evidence for the economist. It fails because the economist already says many applicants knew little about pay; confirming a premise doesn't connect the requirement to the result.

choices.note: Tempting, because it backs up something the economist says. But the economist already asserts it. Confirming a premise adds nothing to the link between the requirement and the narrowing gap.
Wrong. If some employers already listed ranges, the requirement changed less than it seems. If anything, this weakens.
CORRECT. The gap shrank where pay is bargained over and barely where it's fixed. That's exactly the fingerprint the negotiation mechanism predicts, and it's hard to explain by some unrelated trend.
Wrong. More experienced women hires is an alternative explanation for higher starting pay. This weakens.
Wrong. More women hired is about counts, not starting pay. It doesn't show the requirement narrowed the pay gap.

questions.stimulus: Library board member: Advocates of eliminating overdue fines at Tilbury's public libraries claim that doing so would increase borrowing, and they point to a pilot program at the Wexley branch, where borrowing rose after fines were dropped. But the pilot coincided with the opening of a large school next door to the Wexley branch, which by itself could account for the rise. So there is no good reason to believe that eliminating fines would increase borrowing.
questions.stem: The board member's reasoning is flawed in that it
choices: relies on the results at a single branch to draw a conclusion about every one of Tilbury's public libraries
infers that eliminating overdue fines would not increase borrowing from the fact that the advocates' evidence is flawed
takes for granted that the pilot program is the only evidence that could bear on whether ending fines would increase borrowing
presumes, without providing justification, that the opening of the school did in fact cause borrowing at the Wexley branch to rise
takes for granted that results from a pilot program at one branch cannot show anything about the effects of a citywide policy
questions.explanation: The board member shows that the advocates' one piece of evidence is confounded, then concludes there is 'no good reason' at all to expect higher borrowing; that overlooks every other reason or evidence that might exist, as (C) says. (B) is the trap: it describes the textbook 'flawed evidence, so the claim is false' error, but the board member never concludes that borrowing would not rise. (D) misreads 'could account for' as 'did cause,' (A) assigns the advocates' generalization to the board member, and (E) states a view the board member never relies on.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: There is no good reason to believe that eliminating fines would increase borrowing.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Advocates cite the Wexley pilot; but a new school next door could by itself account for Wexley's rise in borrowing.

breakdown.analysis: The board member knocks out one piece of evidence. Fair enough: the school is a real confound. But look at how far the conclusion reaches: 'no good reason' to believe it, period. What about other evidence? Other cities' experience, surveys of people who avoid the library over fines? Knocking out one reason doesn't show there are no reasons. It's like saying: your one witness turned out to be unreliable, so there's no good reason to think the defendant was there. Most students pick (B) because it's the famous flaw: 'the evidence for X is bad, so X is false.' Read the conclusion again. The board member never says borrowing would NOT rise, only that there's no good reason to believe it would. So (B) describes an argument that wasn't made. Know the difference between 'not proven' and 'false.'

choices.note: Wrong party. It's the advocates who generalize from one branch. The board member rejects the pilot as evidence and doesn't rely on it at all.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Borrowing rose at Wexley when fines ended, so ending fines will raise borrowing at every library in Tilbury.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's the classic flaw: treating weak evidence for a claim as proof the claim is false. But the board member's conclusion is weaker: there's 'no good reason to believe' borrowing would rise. That's not the same as saying it wouldn't. This describes a conclusion the board member never drew.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The advocates' only study was flawed, so ending fines would definitely not increase borrowing.

choices.note: CORRECT. The board member eliminates one piece of evidence and concludes there's no good reason at all. That only works if the pilot was the only possible support for the advocates' claim. It wasn't shown to be.
Wrong. The board member says the school 'could account for' the rise, not that it did. Showing a plausible alternative is enough to weaken the pilot as evidence; no proof of cause is presumed.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The new school is next door, so it is obviously what raised borrowing.

choices.note: Wrong. The board member never says pilot programs can't tell us anything about citywide policy. The objection is specific to this pilot: it coincided with the school's opening.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: A single branch is too small a test, so the pilot tells us nothing about the whole system.
